item.title: Getting a First PR Merged into a 75,000-Star Project
item.description: Nine days, four review rounds, three of them asking for changes, and one honest admission. How a fix to Apache Superset got merged, and what the review taught me.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

On 22 September 2026 I opened a pull request against Apache Superset, which has more than 75,000 stars. On 1 October it was merged. In between, a reviewer requested changes three times and two automated reviewers commented as well.

This is about the process. The technical story is in Why Safari exported blank charts.

View this part on the site

What made it a good first issue

  • A clear symptom. "Image export is blank on Safari" is either fixed or not.
  • People affected. The issue had been open since May 2024.
  • A cause that can be explained. The capture library documents Safari as unsupported, and says why. A PR that explains why something broke is much easier to review than one that only makes it stop.

A small fix to an important problem is a better first contribution than a big one to a problem nobody reported.

What to put in the description

Reviewers of large projects read many PRs. The description answered four questions:

  1. What's broken, and for whom?
  2. Why? With a link to the library's own documentation.
  3. What does this change, and what does it deliberately leave alone?
  4. How can you check it?

The third one matters most. Saying "other browsers keep their existing path" tells a reviewer where the risk is not. The first review picked up on exactly that.

Three times "changes requested"

The first review arrived the same day. It called the root-cause analysis correct, and then asked whether map charts would still be blank, because I had skipped a step the old path took. They would have been.

It was a scenario I hadn't covered, from someone who knows what else the code has to do. The pattern repeated:

Round What the review found
1 WebGL charts might still export blank. Load the library lazily. Keep the table print layout
2 Map layers live in a second canvas, which still isn't preserved
3 The capture size and CORS points are resolved. The second canvas is the last blocker
4 Approved, with a request to check on real Safari

Hardly any of it was about style. Behind each blocking point was a user who would still have had the bug.

Answering is part of the work. For each blocking comment I either changed the code and named the commit, or explained why not. One automated reviewer wanted images from other origins included. I replied that allowing them would make the whole export fail, so leaving them out was the better trade. Disagreeing with a reason is fine. Ignoring isn't.

Saying "I can't test this"

Round four asked me to check the result on real Safari. I don't have access to a Mac. I wrote that plainly and asked whether someone else could.

A reviewer did, carefully, and found a problem: the new mode exposed a version mismatch between two of Superset's dependencies. Without an honest "I can't verify this", that test might not have happened before release. The mismatch was in the lockfile rather than in my code, and the main branch has since aligned the versions.

An approval is easy to accept in silence. Saying what you couldn't check is more useful to everyone who will run the code.

What I would do differently

  • Check access to the environment first. For a Safari bug, the first question is "who has Safari?" Ask in the issue before starting.
  • Read the code path around the change. The table layout and the canvas copying that round one asked about were already in the path I had bypassed.
  • Write the failing test first. It forces you to say exactly what's broken. For my later OpenMetadata fix, the tests found two more bugs.
  • Keep commits by concern. Separate commits let reviewers look only at what changed since last time.

If you're about to open your first

  1. Run the project and reproduce the bug before anything else.
  2. Find the contribution guide and the PR template. Follow them literally.
  3. Make the smallest change that fixes the root cause.
  4. Expect several rounds. Requested changes mean someone is taking it seriously.
  5. Reply to every comment, in the code or in words.
  6. Say what you couldn't verify.

GitHub's open source guide covers the basics well, and Superset's contributor documentation is a good example of what large projects expect.

Conclusion

The merged change adds about 150 lines of production code, and more than twice that in tests. The value was in having people who know the system better than I do point at what I couldn't see. You can't get that from a tutorial, and you don't need permission to start.

item.title: I Cut This Site's JavaScript by 45%, and Blocking Time Didn't Move
item.description: Removing 127 KB of JavaScript halved the time to largest paint and did almost nothing for Total Blocking Time. What I measured, what I ruled out, and a font mistake that CI caught.
item.content:encoded:
The plan that should have worked

The previous version of this site shipped 282 KB of gzipped JavaScript on the homepage. Every section was a client component, because each used an animation library and an i18n library. The plan was obvious: move to server components, animate with CSS, ship less.

It worked, partly. Here are the numbers, all from GitHub Pages with Lighthouse's mobile preset on the same machine, three runs before and eight after:

Homepage Before After
JavaScript, gzipped 282 KB 155 KB
Performance score 67–72 79–93
Largest Contentful Paint 4.2–4.3 s 1.7–2.7 s
Total Blocking Time 400–680 ms 280–700 ms

Look at the last row. With 127 KB less JavaScript, you would expect it to fall the most.

What was removed

  • The animation library. Reveal effects are now scroll-driven CSS animations.
  • The translation runtime. Text is resolved while the page is built.
  • State and toast libraries. What was left needed useState.
  • Hydration of static sections. Cards and lists are plain HTML.
@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  .reveal {
    animation: reveal linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0px entry 200px;
  }
}
globals.css

Content is visible by default and the animation is added on top. The old page started at opacity: 0 and waited for scripts. That is why LCP improved so much: the text no longer depends on JavaScript to appear.

Why blocking time stayed

Total Blocking Time adds up the part of each long task beyond 50 ms. It doesn't care how many kilobytes were sent, only how long the main thread was busy at a stretch. So I profiled a local build with a four-times CPU slowdown.

The first suspects were decorative: large blurs, backdrop filters, a noise texture, endless animations. I switched each off in turn and measured again:

Variant Blocking time
Baseline 534 ms
No reveal animations 555 ms
No backdrop filters 600 ms
No blurred shapes 557 ms
No noise or masks 521 ms
No infinite animations 719 ms
content-visibility on sections 520 ms

Each is an average of three runs. Nothing got clearly faster. The one outlier got slower, because it spent longer recalculating styles, most likely due to the rule I injected for the test. The effects that looked expensive cost almost nothing here.

The long tasks were these:

  1. The first style and layout of a long page. Nine sections with many cards is a big tree.
  2. Starting React and hydrating. This is mostly the framework's own cost, and it's the same with two islands or twelve.

Neither is proportional to the code I removed.

Bytes and blocking are different budgets. Removing code buys you download and parse time. It buys main-thread time only if that code was in the long tasks.

The font mistake

Along the way I found that every page preloaded the fonts of both languages, about 110 KB. The bundler had merged the CSS of two layouts. I turned preloading off, and my scores went up:

const sans = Geist({ subsets: ["latin"], preload: false });
ts

Then Lighthouse failed in CI, with a layout shift of 0.14 on a site that had none on my machine. The size-adjusted fallback is based on Arial. My machine has a match for it; the CI runner evidently doesn't, and neither does an Android phone. There, the text moved when the real font arrived.

The real fix was to host the fonts myself, preload only the page's own language, and use font-display: optional, which never swaps after the first paint. Layout shift went back to zero, and stayed there.

Loosening the check would have been one number in a config file. It would also have shipped a regression to every phone without that font.

Then I shortened the page

Less to lay out should attack the largest task directly. So I trimmed the homepage from 1,273 to 1,005 elements, a fifth of the page, and compared old and new builds on a local server, alternating between them, five runs each:

Blocking time, five runs Median
1,273 elements 73, 122, 125, 131, 187 ms 125 ms
1,005 elements 86, 127, 134, 148, 246 ms 134 ms

No difference. A second reasonable theory, and a second one the numbers didn't support. The page is smaller, which is fine, but it isn't faster in this metric.

What I would do next

  • Delay hydration of islands far below the fold, since starting the framework is what remains.
  • Measure real users. Lab numbers on one laptop swing widely: eight runs of the same page gave 280 to 700 ms.

What I'd tell someone starting the same work

  1. Write down the metric you expect to move, before you change anything.
  2. Profile first. I removed the right code for LCP and not the code behind TBT.
  3. Run each measurement several times and publish the range. A single good run is an anecdote.
  4. Keep the check that embarrasses you.

Related: Taming INP, A performance workflow that survives real users and the case study of this site.

item.title: Never Trust JSON.parse in a Render
item.description: One malformed string in a database was enough to crash an OpenMetadata page. How I fixed it upstream with small shape validators, and the two unrelated bugs that writing the tests uncovered.
item.content:encoded:
One bad string, one dead page

OpenMetadata keeps a history of every entity. A version page shows what changed between two versions: tags added, owners removed, a column renamed. Each change stores its old and new values as JSON strings, and the interface parsed them while rendering:

const oldTags: TagLabel[] = JSON.parse(getChangedEntityOldValue(diff) ?? '[]');
ts

That line contains two promises nobody can keep. It promises that the string is valid JSON, and it promises that the JSON is an array of tags. If either fails, the exception happens during render, and React unmounts the tree. The user sees an error page because of one row written long ago.

My fix was merged as pull request #33580.

The type annotation is the trap

JSON.parse returns any. Assigning any to TagLabel[] compiles without a complaint, so the annotation looks like a check and isn't one. It's a comment the compiler believes.

const tags: TagLabel[] = JSON.parse('{"oops": true}'); // compiles
tags.map((t) => t.tagFQN); // TypeError at runtime
ts

The honest return type is unknown. It makes the compiler ask the question you were skipping:

const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(value);
parsed.map(); // error: 'parsed' is of type 'unknown'
ts

Validate at the boundary

View this part on the site

The data crosses a boundary when it's parsed. That's the place to check it, once. After that the rest of the code can rely on the type.

export const parseVersionDiffArray = <T>(
  value?: string,
  isValid: (item: unknown) => boolean = isRecord
): T[] => {
  try {
    const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(value ?? '[]');

    return Array.isArray(parsed) ? (parsed.filter(isValid) as T[]) : [];
  } catch {
    return [];
  }
};
EntityDiffPureUtils.ts

Two decisions here are worth explaining.

It filters instead of rejecting. If one of five tags is malformed, the user should still see the other four. A history page is for reading, so partial data beats none.

It falls back to empty. On a page that writes data I would choose differently: silently treating broken input as empty could overwrite it. Be forgiving when displaying and strict when saving.

Validators that compose

The shapes are small, so plain functions were enough:

export const isTagLabelDiff = (value: unknown) =>
  hasVersionDiffStringProperty(value, 'tagFQN');

export const isNamedEntityWithTagsDiff = (value: unknown) =>
  hasVersionDiffStringProperty(value, 'name') &&
  hasVersionDiffArrayProperty(value, 'tags', isTagLabelDiff);
EntityDiffPureUtils.ts

Schema fields nest: a field has children, which have children. The table that renders them is recursive, so a bad value three levels down crashes it as surely as one at the top. The validator has to recurse as well:

export const isNestedNamedEntityWithTagsDiff = (value: unknown): boolean =>
  isNamedEntityWithTagsDiff(value) &&
  hasVersionDiffArrayProperty(
    value,
    'children',
    isNestedNamedEntityWithTagsDiff
  );
EntityDiffPureUtils.ts

Rule of thumb: the validator should be exactly as deep as the code that consumes the value.

Why not a schema library?

In a new project I would reach for Zod or Valibot: you get the type and the check from one definition. In someone else's large codebase, a bug fix that adds a dependency is a harder conversation than one that adds sixty lines. Match the tool to the change.

The bugs the tests found

The fix was meant to stop crashes. Testing it turned up two problems where nothing crashed at all.

A lookup with the wrong key. Added and deleted search-index fields never appeared on the version page. The code asked for the diff of tasks where it needed fields:

 const fieldsDiff = getDiffByFieldName(
-  EntityField.TASKS,
+  EntityField.FIELDS,
   changeDescription,
   true
 );
diff

The lookup returned nothing, and nothing was rendered. No error, no log.

Pairing by position. ML feature changes matched old and new values by index. That works until one list is filtered, and now lists are filtered. Index 2 on one side is no longer index 2 on the other:

-newDiffs.forEach((newDiff, index) => {
+newDiffs.forEach((newDiff) => {
   if (isEqual(i.name, newDiff.name)) {
+    const oldDiff = oldDiffs.find((o) => o.name === newDiff.name);
     i.description = getTextDiff(
-      oldDiffs[index]?.description ?? '',
+      oldDiff?.description ?? '',
       newDiff.description ?? ''
     );
diff

My own change would have made that second bug worse. If you start dropping items from a list, check everyone who uses its indexes.

Do error boundaries solve this?

They help with a different part. An error boundary turns a blank page into a message, and you should have one. But it can only replace a whole subtree. It can't show the four good tags and skip the bad one. Validation decides what's shown; the boundary is for what you didn't foresee.

Checklist

  1. Search the codebase for JSON.parse( inside components and the functions they call.
  2. Replace any with unknown at each one.
  3. Decide per place: drop the item, use a default, or stop.
  4. Write the test with the malformed value first, and watch it crash.
  5. Include null, an object where an array is expected, and a nested bad child.

Conclusion

Anything that comes from storage, a network or localStorage was written by some other version of your software. Parse it as if a stranger wrote it. For types that help after the boundary, see TypeScript as a programming language.

item.title: What Persian Users See in Two Open-Source Data Tools
item.description: I ran Apache Superset and OpenMetadata in Persian and measured what changed. The layout doesn't turn around, some translations mean something else, and one language code may explain the strangest results.
item.content:encoded:
Two tools, one question

More than two billion people use Arabic-script languages, according to a recent study of chart tools. It tested seven tools, and none of them was Apache Superset or OpenMetadata, the two I contribute to. So I ran both in Persian, with a small Persian dataset, and measured what happened. The report card has every result and screenshot.

The layout doesn't turn around

After switching to Persian, neither Superset 6.1.0 nor OpenMetadata 1.12.14 set a direction on the page. The navigation stayed on the left. Every Persian text sat in a left-to-right container, which shows in small ways: the full stop moves to the wrong end of a sentence, and a long title loses its first letters instead of its last.

This is known. Superset's RTL issue is closed as mostly done, and a pull request that aimed to finish it was closed unmerged after the theme code it depended on had changed several times. OpenMetadata fixed a direction regression this month, after the version I tested.

Translated isn't the same as correct

Superset's Persian file has 5,957 entries. 2,473 of them are marked fuzzy, which means unreviewed: 1,569 come from a machine translation that says so in a comment, and 904 were guessed from similar sentences. Release 6.1.0 includes fuzzy entries when it builds translations. The guesses can be far off:

English What the Persian says
Enter the user's password Enter the alert name
The password reset was successful This dashboard was saved successfully
(Removed) Dear assistant, your task doesn't contain any text for translation

The last one isn't fuzzy. It's a reply from a chatbot, saved as a translation.

A language code that may explain a mystery

OpenMetadata's Persian file contains Spanish ("Acción requerida"), Portuguese ("Salvar alterações"), Turkish, Pashto, Arabic and, in a few places, pirate English:

Shiver me timbers! Error fetchin' the treasures…

These are checked against the file as it was on 24 November 2026. The file is called pr-pr.json. The code for Persian is fa. My guess, and it is a guess, is that tools filling in missing strings read pr-PR as Puerto Rico, as Portuguese, or as pirate. Of its 7,243 entries, 188 contain no Persian, and 322 are identical to English.

How to check your own project

  1. Use standard codes. fa, ar, he. Tools make decisions based on them.
  2. Set lang and dir on the document when the language changes.
  3. Look for one translation shared by several sources. In Superset, that found 461 entries worth reading.
  4. Check the script. A Persian file should contain Persian letters.
  5. Don't ship what's marked unreviewed, or show which strings are.

The scripts need only Python and a browser.

What this is not

It's a pilot: two tools, desktop only, default settings, no keyboard or screen reader testing. Both projects are free, and both have accepted fixes from me. If you work on either one, the review lists are there to use.

item.title: Resumable Uploads: What Happens When the Connection Drops
item.description: A large upload will be interrupted. This article walks through the TUS protocol request by request, with a live demo you can break, and the client-side decisions that make resuming reliable.
item.content:encoded:
The problem with one big request

Uploading a file is one line of code, until the file is large. A 3 GB CSV over a 20 Mbit/s connection takes about twenty minutes. Somewhere in those minutes a laptop sleeps, a VPN reconnects or a proxy times out. With a single POST, all progress is lost.

I built an upload module for a data platform, designed for files of several gigabytes. This article covers the ideas behind it. The demo is a separate example that uses the same libraries.

Why "just split it into chunks" isn't enough

The obvious fix is to slice the file and send the pieces. Then the questions begin. Which pieces arrived? What if a piece arrived but its response didn't? Who deletes the pieces of an upload nobody finished?

Those are protocol questions, and answering them privately means maintaining both ends forever. TUS is an open protocol that answers them, with clients and servers in many languages. The IETF is standardizing the same idea as resumable uploads for HTTP.

Three requests

View this part on the site

Create. The client announces the size and gets a URL for this upload.

POST /files HTTP/1.1
Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0
Upload-Length: 50331648

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /files/24e533e
http

Send. A PATCH carries bytes, and says where they start.

PATCH /files/24e533e HTTP/1.1
Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0
Upload-Offset: 0
Content-Type: application/offset+octet-stream
http

Ask. After any interruption, HEAD returns what the server actually stored.

HEAD /files/24e533e HTTP/1.1
Tus-Resumable: 1.0.0

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Upload-Offset: 12163470
http

The next PATCH starts at that offset. If the client gets it wrong, the server answers 409 Conflict instead of corrupting the file.

Try to break it

The demo runs the real tus-js-client through Uppy, against a small TUS server that lives in this tab. Start an upload and drop the connection halfway.

View this part on the site

Look at the log after a drop. The number in the last HEAD and the number in the following PATCH are always the same. A test checks exactly that before every deploy of this site.

Decisions on the client

The server is the only source of truth

A progress bar shows bytes sent. Bytes sent aren't bytes stored: some were in flight when the connection died. Never resume from the progress value. Ask.

Never load the file into memory

File is a Blob, and Blob.slice() is lazy. It returns a view without reading anything, so a resumed upload of a 3 GB file costs almost no memory:

const offset = Number(response.headers.get("Upload-Offset"));
const rest = file.slice(offset); // no bytes read yet
await fetch(uploadUrl, {
  method: "PATCH",
  headers: {
    "Tus-Resumable": "1.0.0",
    "Upload-Offset": String(offset),
    "Content-Type": "application/offset+octet-stream",
  },
  body: rest,
});
js

The mistake to avoid is await file.arrayBuffer(), which reads all of it.

Retry with growing delays, and know when to stop

Retrying immediately makes an overloaded server worse. Growing delays give the network time, and a limit gives the user an answer:

new Uppy().use(Tus, {
  endpoint: "/files",
  retryDelays: [0, 1000, 3000, 5000, 10000],
});
js

Not every failure deserves a retry. A 403 will be a 403 again in five seconds. Network errors, 409, 423 and 5xx are worth retrying; other 4xx responses aren't.

Pausing is not failing

A user who presses pause and a network that disappears look similar to the code, but mean different things. One should wait without limit. The other should retry. Keep them as separate states in the interface too, so nobody wonders whether anything is happening:

State Who ends it What to show
Uploading the server progress
Paused the user a resume button
Retrying a timer that it will continue by itself
Failed the user the reason, and a retry button

Do you need chunks at all?

TUS doesn't require them. One PATCH can carry the whole remainder, and the server keeps what it received if it breaks. Set chunkSize only when something in between forces you to, such as a proxy with a body limit. Small chunks add a round trip each.

What the server has to do

  • Store the offset durably before acknowledging it.
  • Reject a PATCH whose offset doesn't match.
  • Expire unfinished uploads, or storage fills with halves of files.
  • Check that the user resuming an upload is the one who created it. The URL alone must not be a permission.

Conclusion

Resuming isn't a feature you add to an upload. It's a question, "how much do you have?", asked of the only party that knows. Once the protocol asks it, pause, retry and recovery stop being special cases.

The case study has the product side. For another place where the main thread matters during heavy file work, see Web Workers in practice.

item.title: RTL Is Not a Translation Step
item.description: Right-to-left support isn't a mirrored stylesheet added at the end. Logical properties, text isolation, icons, fonts and numbers: the parts of an interface that change direction, and the parts that must not.
item.content:encoded:
The usual mistake

A product is finished in English. Then someone asks for Persian or Arabic, so the strings go to a translator and a dir="rtl" goes on the page. Half of the layout flips, the other half doesn't, and file paths read backwards.

I led the Persian localization of a data platform, and this site is bilingual too. The lesson from both is the same: translation changes words, while direction changes layout. They are different jobs.

Write direction-neutral CSS from the start

Physical properties name sides of the screen. Logical properties name sides of the text. Only one of them survives a direction change.

Physical Logical
margin-left margin-inline-start
padding-right padding-inline-end
border-left border-inline-start
left: 0 inset-inline-start: 0
text-align: left text-align: start
border-top-left-radius border-start-start-radius

Flexbox and grid already follow direction. A row starts on the right in an RTL page without any change. Most broken layouts come from a physical margin left inside a logical container.

Try it. Compare the two styles, then switch the direction:

View this part on the site

If you use Tailwind, the same idea is ms-*, me-*, ps-*, pe-*, start-* and end-*. Adding a lint rule against the physical versions is cheaper than a review comment on every pull request.

Text has its own direction

The Unicode bidirectional algorithm decides the order of mixed text. Letters have a strong direction. Punctuation, spaces and slashes are neutral and take their direction from their neighbours. That's why a path like /data/2026/report (final).csv falls apart inside a Persian sentence: its slashes and brackets get adopted by the Persian text around them.

The fix is isolation. Tell the algorithm that a run of text is an island:

<!-- direction known -->
<bdi dir="ltr">/data/2026/report (final).csv</bdi>

<!-- direction unknown: user names, titles, search terms -->
<bdi>{userName}</bdi>
<p dir="auto">{comment}</p>
html

In a data product, isolate these by default: column names, SQL, file paths, URLs, email addresses, versions and keyboard shortcuts. Code blocks and terminals stay left-to-right inside a right-to-left page. Set dir="ltr" on them.

For form fields, dir="auto" follows whatever the user types. An email field should be dir="ltr" always, even when its label is Persian.

Not everything mirrors

Mirror Don't mirror
Back and forward arrows Play and pause
Breadcrumb separators Clocks and circular progress
Progress bars, sliders Logos
Indentation, tree views Charts with a time axis (ask your users)
Send icon Checkmarks, search

A direction variant keeps this in one place:

[dir="rtl"] .icon-directional {
  transform: scaleX(-1);
}
css

Use scaleX(-1) rather than rotate(180deg) for anything asymmetric. A rotated paper-plane icon is upside down.

Transforms don't know about direction

Logical properties cover layout, not transforms. translateX(20px) moves right in every language, so a drawer that slides in from the start needs a sign:

.drawer { --dir: 1; transform: translateX(calc(-100% * var(--dir))); }
[dir="rtl"] .drawer { --dir: -1; }
css

The same goes for scroll positions in JavaScript. In RTL containers scrollLeft starts at 0 and becomes negative. Carousel code with scrollLeft += width needs the same sign.

Fonts and spacing

Persian and Arabic letters join. Negative letter-spacing, popular for large headings, breaks the joins and looks like a rendering bug. On this site one rule prevents it:

html[lang="fa"] body *:not(:lang(en)):not([dir="ltr"]) {
  letter-spacing: 0 !important;
}
css

Also check line height. Arabic-script letters have tall marks and deep descenders, and a heading set at line-height: 1 will clip them. text-transform: uppercase does nothing in these scripts, so a design that relies on capitals for hierarchy needs another signal.

Numbers, dates and plurals

Digits are a locale choice. Let the platform make it:

new Intl.NumberFormat("fa-IR").format(15859);  // ۱۵٬۸۵۹
new Intl.DateTimeFormat("fa-IR").format(date); // Solar Hijri calendar
js

Decide where not to localize. Identifiers, version numbers and code should keep Latin digits, because people copy them.

Never assemble sentences from fragments. "Page " + n + " of " + total can't be reordered by a translator. Use one string with placeholders.

Test it like a layout, not like a translation

  • Screenshots in both directions for each component. Most bugs are visible at a glance.
  • Pseudo-RTL in English. Set dir="rtl" on the English build. You find layout bugs before any translation exists.
  • Mixed content. Test with a Persian sentence that contains a path, a number and an English product name.
  • Keyboard. In a right-to-left tab list, the left arrow goes to the next tab.

On this site, the same automated tests check pages in both languages for horizontal overflow and accessibility problems.

Conclusion

If the layout is written in terms of start and end, RTL is mostly a configuration value. If it's written in terms of left and right, RTL is a rewrite. The choice is made long before anyone asks for a second language.

Further reading: MDN on logical properties, the W3C's guide to inline bidi markup, and Translating forms generated from JSON Schema.

item.title: Why Safari Exported Blank Charts in Apache Superset
item.description: A chart export that worked everywhere except Safari led through SVG foreignObject, WebGL drawing buffers and tainted canvases. Here is the root cause, the fix that was merged, and the part I got wrong.
item.content:encoded:
A bug that only existed in one engine

In Apache Superset you can download a chart or a whole dashboard as an image. On Safari the file came out blank, or partly blank. The issue had been open since May 2024. Chrome and Firefox were fine.

A bug that follows the engine instead of the data is a useful hint. The application code is the same everywhere, so something below it must differ. The job is to find out which step.

How a DOM node becomes a PNG

Browsers have no "screenshot this element" API for pages, so libraries emulate one. Superset uses dom-to-image-more, which works like this:

View this part on the site

  1. Clone the DOM node and copy its computed styles inline.
  2. Put the clone into an SVG, inside a <foreignObject>. That element exists to embed HTML in SVG.
  3. Load the SVG as an image and draw it to a canvas.
  4. Read the canvas with toDataURL().

Step 2 is where WebKit stops. It applies a stricter security model to foreignObject content and refuses to paint it, so the canvas in step 3 stays empty. Nothing throws. toDataURL() happily encodes an empty canvas.

The library's own README lists Safari as unsupported for this reason. That changes the shape of the problem: there is no missing option to find. No setting in this library can work.

Choosing a fix you can defend

There were three candidates.

Option Problem
Replace the library for everyone Puts working exports on Chrome and Firefox at risk
Tell Safari users it isn't supported The issue had been open for two years already
Use a different rasterizer on Safari only Two code paths to maintain

I chose the third. html2canvas reads the DOM and paints it itself, without foreignObject. It was already installed as a dependency of another package, so promoting it added nothing new to the tree. And it loads only where it's needed:

if (isSafari()) {
  // Stays out of the core bundle: only Safari ever downloads it
  const { default: html2canvas } = await import('html2canvas');
  const canvas = await html2canvas(element, captureOptions);
  triggerDownload(canvas.toDataURL(type, quality), description, isPng);
  return;
}
downloadAsImage.tsx

The pull request started out this small. Review showed how much was missing.

Problem two: content that isn't visible yet

Superset tables are virtualized: only the rows on screen exist in the DOM. The existing path switches ag-grid to its print layout before capturing, then restores it. My first version returned early and skipped all of that, so long tables would have been cut off. The final version keeps the whole lifecycle and replaces only the rasterizing step.

A related bug was more subtle. I measured the element, then expanded its clipped content inside the clone. The canvas was therefore sized for the collapsed version. html2canvas reads its dimensions after the onclone callback, so the fix is to widen them there:

onclone: (_document, clone) => {
  processCloneForVisibility(clone, isDashboardCapture);
  preserveCanvasContent(elementToPrint, clone, getInstanceByDom);
  captureOptions.width = Math.max(captureOptions.width ?? 0, clone.scrollWidth);
  captureOptions.height = Math.max(captureOptions.height ?? 0, clone.scrollHeight);
},
downloadAsImage.tsx

Math.max keeps the on-screen size as a floor, so a clone that can't be measured never makes the result smaller.

Problem three: WebGL canvases read back empty

A cloned <canvas> is blank, because cloning copies the element and not its pixels. For 2D canvases you copy the pixels with drawImage. WebGL adds a catch: after a frame is presented, the browser may clear the drawing buffer. Read it later and you get nothing.

The fix is a context option, preserveDrawingBuffer. It has a cost, so it's set only on Safari.

deck.gl needed one more step. It drew its layers into a second canvas laid over the map, with its own context and its own unpreserved buffer. A chart would have exported the map without the data. In interleaved mode deck.gl renders into the base map's context instead, so one preserved buffer holds everything.

Problem four: images you aren't allowed to read

An image from another origin without CORS headers taints a canvas. A tainted canvas refuses toDataURL(), so one logo could break the entire export. A review bot flagged that such images would be missing. I kept useCORS: true and tainting off: the inaccessible image is left out, and everything else exports. That is also what the old path did.

What I got wrong

I don't have access to a Mac, and jsdom can't render WebGL. My tests prove that interleaved reaches the component on Safari. They can't prove that a heatmap appears.

A reviewer tested on real Safari and found that interleaved mode exposed a version mismatch in the lockfile: the deck.gl map adapter called a method that the installed deck.gl core didn't have. Superset's main branch has since moved both packages to the same version.

A test that checks configuration tells you the switch was flipped. It doesn't tell you the light came on.

What to take from it

  • Silent failures deserve suspicion. An empty canvas is valid data to every later step.
  • Read the library's support table early. It rules out every option that could never have worked.
  • Contain the change. Browsers that already worked kept their exact path.
  • Ask who can run it. If you can't test the engine you're fixing, arrange that before you open the PR.

The shorter version of this story is in the case study, and the human side is in Getting a first PR merged into a large project.

item.title: Translating Forms Generated from JSON Schema
item.description: When forms are generated from a schema, their labels aren't in your translation files. A practical approach: extract text by path, translate it in a catalog, and localize the schema before it reaches the form.
item.content:encoded:
Text that isn't in your code

Data platforms connect to dozens of systems, and each has its own settings. Nobody writes those forms by hand. They're generated from JSON Schema: a field's title becomes its label and description becomes its help text.

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "hostPort": {
      "title": "Host and Port",
      "description": "Host and port of the PostgreSQL service.",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "sslMode": {
      "title": "SSL Mode",
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["disable", "require", "verify-full"]
    }
  },
  "required": ["hostPort"]
}
postgres.json

Then you localize the product. Your translation files cover every string in your components, and the connection form is still in English. The text comes from a schema, often written by a backend team, sometimes in another repository.

I worked on this while localizing an OpenMetadata-based platform into Persian. The code below is a simplified illustration of the approach, not the product's source.

Three ways that don't last

Edit the schemas. They're generated or owned by someone else, and the next upgrade overwrites you.

Translate in the form's templates. Looking up t(label) with the English text as the key works until two fields share a title. "Name" might need different words for a person and a database.

Keep a copy of each schema per language. The copies drift. A new required field appears in English and not in Persian, and the form starts sending invalid data.

Translate the schema, not the form

The idea that holds up: treat a schema as data, pull its text out into a catalog, and put translated text back just before rendering. The form generator never knows.

View this part on the site

Step 1: extract by path

A JSON Pointer identifies a piece of text uniquely, so "Name" in two places has two keys:

const TEXT_KEYS = ["title", "description"] as const;

export function extract(node: unknown, path = "", out: Record<string, string> = {}) {
  if (Array.isArray(node)) node.forEach((item, i) => extract(item, `${path}/${i}`, out));
  else if (node && typeof node === "object") {
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(node)) {
      if (isTextKey(key) && typeof value === "string" && !isPropertyMap(path)) out[`${path}/${key}`] = value;
      else extract(value, `${path}/${key}`, out);
    }
  }
  return out;
}

const isTextKey = (key: string) => (TEXT_KEYS as readonly string[]).includes(key);

/** Inside "properties", keys are field names. A field may itself be called "title". */
const isPropertyMap = (path: string) => /\/(properties|\$defs|definitions)$/.test(path);
extract.ts

That last function matters. Under properties, the word title is the name of a field, not text. Forget it and a schema with a field called description is silently damaged.

Step 2: a catalog people can review

{
  "/properties/hostPort/title": "میزبان و درگاه",
  "/properties/sslMode/title": "حالت SSL"
}
fa/postgres.json

Store the English source next to each translation, or a hash of it. When the source text changes, the entry is marked for review instead of being quietly wrong.

Step 3: localize a copy

export function localize<T>(schema: T, catalog: Record<string, string>): T {
  const copy = structuredClone(schema);
  for (const [pointer, text] of Object.entries(catalog)) {
    const keys = pointer.slice(1).split("/");
    const last = keys.pop()!;
    const parent = keys.reduce<any>((node, key) => node?.[key], copy);
    if (parent && typeof parent[last] === "string") parent[last] = text;
  }
  return copy;
}
localize.ts

(A full JSON Pointer also escapes / as ~1 in names. Add that if your field names contain slashes.)

If a pointer no longer exists, it's skipped, and the field stays in English. A half-translated form is usable. A crashed one isn't.

const localized = useMemo(() => localize(schema, catalogs[locale]), [schema, locale]);
return <Form schema={localized} formData={data} />;
ConnectionForm.tsx

Never translate values

enum values are data. Translate verify-full and the backend rejects the form. Give options a label instead. In JSON Schema that's oneOf with const and title:

{
  "sslMode": {
    "oneOf": [
      { "const": "disable", "title": "غیرفعال" },
      { "const": "require", "title": "الزامی" }
    ]
  }
}
json

The same goes for property names, $id, format and patterns. A short allow-list of text keys is safer than a long list of exceptions.

Validation messages

Validators such as Ajv produce English errors from the schema's keywords. Translate by keyword and fill in parameters, so one message covers all fields:

const messages = {
  required: (p) => `وارد کردن ${p.label} الزامی است`,
  minLength: (p) => `${p.label} باید حداقل ${p.limit} نویسه باشد`,
};
ts

Use the localized title as label, not the property name. hostPort in the middle of a Persian sentence is both unclear and, because of text direction, oddly placed.

Direction inside the form

Labels are Persian. Values mostly aren't: hosts, connection strings, SQL, JSON. Let the schema decide the direction of each input:

const inputDir = (field) =>
  ["uri", "email", "hostname"].includes(field.format) || field.writeOnly ? "ltr" : "auto";
ts

More on why that matters in RTL is not a translation step.

Keep it honest in CI

Three checks are cheap and catch nearly everything:

  1. Coverage: every extracted pointer has a translation, or is listed as pending.
  2. Dead entries: every catalog pointer still exists in the schema.
  3. Structure: after removing text keys, the localized schema equals the original. This one proves that translation never changes what the form accepts.
expect(stripText(localize(schema, fa))).toEqual(stripText(schema));
ts

Conclusion

Generated interfaces need generated translation. Once text is addressed by path, a new connector is translated by adding a file, and an upgrade shows you exactly which sentences changed.

item.title: Async Iterators, Generators and Web Streams in Practice
item.description: Process data incrementally instead of all at once. A practical tour of generators, async iteration, backpressure, and the Web Streams API — with examples for paginated APIs, streaming fetch responses and LLM-style token streams.
item.content:encoded:
Why incremental processing matters

Loading a 200MB CSV into memory before showing anything, or waiting for a whole LLM response before rendering a word, are both symptoms of one habit: treating data as a single value instead of a sequence over time. JavaScript has three tools for sequences: generators, async iterators and streams.

Generators: pausable functions

A generator function returns an iterator. Each yield pauses execution until the consumer asks for the next value:

function* range(start, end, step = 1) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i;
}

for (const n of range(0, 10, 3)) console.log(n); // 0 3 6 9
js

Because they're lazy, generators can describe infinite sequences and compose without creating intermediate arrays:

function* map(iter, fn) { for (const x of iter) yield fn(x); }
function* filter(iter, fn) { for (const x of iter) if (fn(x)) yield x; }
function* take(iter, n) {
  if (n <= 0) return;
  for (const x of iter) {
    yield x;
    if (--n <= 0) return; // closes the source iterator too
  }
}

function* naturals() { let n = 0; while (true) yield n++; }

const firstFiveEvenSquares = [...take(filter(map(naturals(), (n) => n * n), (n) => n % 2 === 0), 5)];
// [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]
js

Modern engines also ship iterator helpers natively, so the same pipeline can be written as naturals().map(...).filter(...).take(5).toArray().

Async generators: sequences that arrive over time

Add async and you can await inside and yield values as they become available. Consumers use for await...of.

A classic use: hiding pagination behind a simple loop.

async function* fetchAllIssues(repo) {
  let url = `https://api.github.com/repos/${repo}/issues?per_page=100`;
  while (url) {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    yield* await res.json();                       // yield each issue individually
    url = parseNextLink(res.headers.get("link"));  // null when there are no more pages
  }
}

for await (const issue of fetchAllIssues("facebook/react")) {
  if (issue.title.includes("hydration")) {
    console.log(issue.number, issue.title);
    break; // stops fetching further pages
  }
}
js

That break matters: leaving a for await loop calls the generator's return(), which runs any finally blocks. Pages after the one you needed are never requested. The consumer controls the pace — that's pull-based backpressure.

Cleanup with finally

Generators are a natural place to tie resource lifetime to iteration:

async function* watchEvents(url) {
  const source = new EventSource(url);
  const queue = [];
  let notify;
  source.onmessage = (e) => { queue.push(JSON.parse(e.data)); notify?.(); };
  try {
    while (true) {
      while (queue.length) yield queue.shift();
      await new Promise((r) => (notify = r));
    }
  } finally {
    source.close(); // runs on break, return or throw
  }
}
js

Web Streams: the platform's streaming primitive

ReadableStream, WritableStream and TransformStream are standard in browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun and edge runtimes. fetch response bodies are ReadableStreams, which means you can process a download as it arrives:

const res = await fetch("/api/large-export.ndjson");

const lines = res.body
  .pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream())   // bytes -> text chunks
  .pipeThrough(splitLines());             // text chunks -> lines

let count = 0;
for await (const line of lines) {         // ReadableStream is async iterable
  if (!line) continue;
  const record = JSON.parse(line);
  count++;
  if (count % 1000 === 0) renderProgress(count);
}
js

The splitLines transform buffers partial lines across chunk boundaries — the classic streaming bug to avoid:

function splitLines() {
  let buffer = "";
  return new TransformStream({
    transform(chunk, controller) {
      buffer += chunk;
      const lines = buffer.split("\n");
      buffer = lines.pop(); // the last item may be an incomplete line
      for (const line of lines) controller.enqueue(line);
    },
    flush(controller) {
      if (buffer) controller.enqueue(buffer);
    },
  });
}
js

Async iteration of ReadableStream is supported in Node, Deno, Firefox and recent Chromium. Where it's missing, use stream.getReader() and call read() in a loop.

Streaming text into the UI

The same technique renders streamed AI responses token by token:

function useStreamedText(url, body) {
  const [text, setText] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    (async () => {
      const res = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body, signal: controller.signal });
      const stream = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream());
      for await (const chunk of stream) {
        setText((prev) => prev + chunk);
      }
    })().catch((err) => {
      if (err.name !== "AbortError") console.error(err);
    });
    return () => controller.abort(); // cancels the request on unmount
  }, [url, body]);

  return text;
}
jsx

AbortController is the cancellation signal for the whole pipeline: aborting the fetch cancels the stream, which ends the for await loop.

View this part on the site

Producing streams

You can create streams from any source, including an async generator:

function fromAsyncIterable(iterable) {
  const iterator = iterable[Symbol.asyncIterator]();
  return new ReadableStream({
    async pull(controller) {
      const { value, done } = await iterator.next();
      done ? controller.close() : controller.enqueue(value);
    },
    async cancel(reason) {
      await iterator.return?.(reason);
    },
  });
}
js

Using pull (instead of pushing everything in start) means the generator only advances when the consumer has room in its queue, so backpressure flows from the consumer back to the source. Newer runtimes provide ReadableStream.from(iterable) which does this for you.

On the server, a streamed Response is just a stream in the body:

// Route handler (Next.js, Remix, Hono, Workers...)
export async function GET() {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
  async function* events() {
    for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));
      yield encoder.encode(`data: tick ${i}\n\n`);
    }
  }
  return new Response(fromAsyncIterable(events()), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "text/event-stream" },
  });
}
js

Choosing the right tool

Need Use
Lazy, synchronous sequence Generator / iterator helpers
Values that arrive over time, consumer-paced Async generator + for await
Bytes or text across network/file boundaries, piping, compression Web Streams (pipeThrough, CompressionStream)
Cancellation AbortController + break / return()

Conclusion

When you model data as a sequence over time, users see the first result sooner, memory stays flat regardless of input size, and cancellation works naturally. Generators make sequences easy to write, async iteration makes them easy to consume, and Web Streams connect them to the network on every modern JavaScript runtime.

Further reading

  • Streams API on MDN
  • for await...of on MDN
  • Streams Standard
  • Resumable uploads: what happens when the connection drops
  • Inside the JavaScript event loop

item.title: The Browser Rendering Pipeline: Writing 60fps Animations
item.description: Style, layout, paint and composite — what each stage costs, which CSS properties trigger which stages, and how to build animations that stay smooth with transforms, will-change, FLIP and the View Transitions API.
item.content:encoded:
The pixel pipeline

Every frame the browser produces goes through up to five stages:

JavaScript → Style → Layout → Paint → Composite
text
  1. JavaScript — your code (or CSS animations/transitions) changes something.
  2. Style — the browser works out which CSS rules apply to which elements and computes final styles.
  3. Layout — it calculates the geometry of every affected box: size and position.
  4. Paint — it records drawing commands (text, colours, borders, shadows, images) for each layer.
  5. Composite — layers are rasterised (often on the GPU) and assembled into the final image.

At 60Hz you have 16.7ms per frame for all of this, and in practice closer to 10ms of budget for your own work. At 120Hz it's 8.3ms.

The key optimisation insight: later stages are cheaper, and you can skip earlier ones.

View this part on the site

Which properties trigger which stages

You change… Layout Paint Composite
width, height, top, left, margin, padding, font-size ✅ ✅ ✅
color, background-color, box-shadow, border-radius — ✅ ✅
transform, opacity (on a composited layer) — — ✅

Animating left from 0 to 300px re-runs layout and paint every frame. Animating transform: translateX() across the same distance only needs compositing — which can even run on the compositor thread while the main thread is busy.

/* ❌ Layout + paint every frame */
.drawer { transition: left 300ms ease; }
.drawer.open { left: 0; }

/* ✅ Composite only */
.drawer { transition: transform 300ms ease; transform: translateX(-100%); }
.drawer.open { transform: translateX(0); }
css

Layers and will-change

To composite an element on its own, the browser must promote it to a layer. Elements with active transform/opacity animations get promoted automatically, but promotion at animation start can cause a one-frame hitch. will-change tells the browser ahead of time:

.card:hover { will-change: transform; }
css

Use it sparingly:

  • Every layer costs GPU memory. Putting will-change: transform on hundreds of list items can make performance worse, especially on mobile.
  • Prefer adding it just before an animation (on hover, or from JS right before starting) and removing it afterwards.
  • Layer promotion changes stacking and can affect text anti-aliasing.

Forced synchronous layout (layout thrashing)

Browsers batch style and layout work until the end of the frame. But if you read a layout property (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), scrollTop…) after writing a style, the browser must calculate layout immediately to give you a correct answer.

// ❌ Each iteration: write → read → forced layout
items.forEach((item) => {
  item.style.width = container.offsetWidth / 3 + "px";
});

// ✅ Read once, then write
const width = container.offsetWidth / 3;
items.forEach((item) => {
  item.style.width = width + "px";
});
js

DevTools' Performance panel flags these as purple Layout blocks with a "Forced reflow" warning, pointing to the line that caused them.

The FLIP technique

Some animations seem to require animating layout — reordering a list, expanding a card into a modal. FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) turns them into cheap transforms:

function flip(element, mutate) {
  // First: record the starting position
  const first = element.getBoundingClientRect();

  // Apply the DOM/layout change instantly
  mutate();

  // Last: record the final position
  const last = element.getBoundingClientRect();

  // Invert: move it back to where it started using a transform
  const dx = first.left - last.left;
  const dy = first.top - last.top;
  const sx = first.width / last.width;
  const sy = first.height / last.height;

  // Play: animate the transform back to identity
  element.animate(
    [
      { transformOrigin: "top left", transform: `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px) scale(${sx}, ${sy})` },
      { transformOrigin: "top left", transform: "none" },
    ],
    { duration: 400, easing: "cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)" }
  );
}
js

The expensive layout happens once, and the animation itself is composite-only. This is exactly what Framer Motion's layout prop does under the hood.

The View Transitions API

For transitions between whole UI states — or even between pages — the browser can now do the FLIP work for you:

function updateView(render) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) return render();
  document.startViewTransition(() => render());
}
js
/* Give elements a shared identity across the two states */
.product-thumb { view-transition-name: product-hero; }

/* Customise the default cross-fade */
::view-transition-old(root),
::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation-duration: 250ms;
}
css

The browser snapshots the old state, runs your update, snapshots the new state and animates between them with pseudo-elements. Elements that share a view-transition-name morph from one position and size to the other. Cross-document view transitions (for multi-page apps) are enabled with a CSS opt-in: @view-transition { navigation: auto; }.

Paint cost is real too

Even without layout, some paints are expensive:

  • Large box-shadow and filter: blur() values, especially when animated.
  • backdrop-filter over large or frequently changing areas.
  • Huge areas invalidated by small changes. Use DevTools → Rendering → Paint flashing to see what repaints.

A useful trick for animated shadows: put the shadow on a pseudo-element and animate its opacity instead of the shadow itself.

.card { position: relative; }
.card::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  box-shadow: 0 20px 40px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.2);
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 200ms;
}
.card:hover::after { opacity: 1; }
css

Containment

The contain property tells the browser an element's internals don't affect the outside, so it can limit how far style, layout and paint work spreads:

.widget { contain: layout paint; }
.offscreen-section { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 600px; }
css

content-visibility: auto skips rendering off-screen subtrees entirely — often the biggest single win on long pages.

Respect user preferences

Smooth isn't the same as necessary. Users with vestibular disorders can be made physically unwell by large motion:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}
css

Conclusion

Animate transform and opacity, batch layout reads before writes, use FLIP or View Transitions when layout really must change, and keep layers and expensive paints under control. Once you know which pipeline stages each change triggers, hitting 60fps (or 120fps) becomes a design decision rather than luck.

Further reading

  • Rendering performance on web.dev
  • CSS containment on MDN
  • View Transition API on MDN
  • Inside the JavaScript event loop
  • I cut this site's JavaScript by 45%, and blocking time didn't move

item.title: Building a Fine-Grained Reactivity System (Signals) From Scratch
item.description: Signals power Solid, Preact, Angular and Vue's reactivity. Build one in under 100 lines to understand dependency tracking, computed values, effects and glitch-free updates.
item.content:encoded:
Why signals are everywhere

Solid, Preact Signals, Angular, Vue, Svelte 5 runes and the TC39 Signals proposal all share one idea: track exactly which computations read which values, and re-run only those when a value changes. Instead of re-rendering a component tree and diffing, a signal-based UI updates the one text node that depends on the changed value.

The best way to understand it is to build one. We'll write signal, computed and effect in plain JavaScript.

View this part on the site

Step 1: a signal is a value with subscribers

let currentObserver = null;

export function signal(initial) {
  let value = initial;
  const subscribers = new Set();

  const read = () => {
    // Auto-tracking: whoever is running right now depends on us
    if (currentObserver) {
      subscribers.add(currentObserver);
      currentObserver.dependencies.add(subscribers);
    }
    return value;
  };

  const write = (next) => {
    if (Object.is(next, value)) return;
    value = next;
    // Copy first: running effects may modify the set
    for (const sub of [...subscribers]) sub.schedule();
  };

  return [read, write];
}
js

The key trick is currentObserver: a global pointer to "the computation currently executing". Any signal read while it's set records a dependency. This is automatic dependency tracking — no dependency arrays.

Step 2: effects

An effect runs a function, tracking everything it reads. When any of those change, it re-runs.

function cleanup(observer) {
  for (const dep of observer.dependencies) dep.delete(observer);
  observer.dependencies.clear();
}

export function effect(fn) {
  const observer = {
    dependencies: new Set(),
    schedule() {
      run();
    },
  };

  function run() {
    cleanup(observer); // dependencies can change between runs
    const prev = currentObserver;
    currentObserver = observer;
    try {
      fn();
    } finally {
      currentObserver = prev;
    }
  }

  run();
  return () => cleanup(observer); // dispose
}
js

Why cleanup before every run? Consider conditional reads:

const [showName, setShowName] = signal(true);
const [name, setName] = signal("Ada");

effect(() => {
  console.log(showName() ? name() : "hidden");
});

setShowName(false); // logs "hidden"
setName("Grace");   // should NOT re-run — name is no longer read
js

Re-collecting dependencies on each run means the effect stops listening to name once the branch that read it is gone. This dynamic dependency tracking is something React's static dependency arrays can't express.

Step 3: computed values

A computed is both an observer (it reads signals) and a source (others read it). It should be lazy and cached: only recompute when read and stale.

export function computed(fn) {
  let value;
  let dirty = true;
  const subscribers = new Set();

  const observer = {
    dependencies: new Set(),
    schedule() {
      if (dirty) return;
      dirty = true;
      // Propagate staleness, don't recompute yet
      for (const sub of [...subscribers]) sub.schedule();
    },
  };

  return () => {
    if (currentObserver) {
      subscribers.add(currentObserver);
      currentObserver.dependencies.add(subscribers);
    }
    if (dirty) {
      cleanup(observer);
      const prev = currentObserver;
      currentObserver = observer;
      try {
        value = fn();
      } finally {
        currentObserver = prev;
      }
      dirty = false;
    }
    return value;
  };
}
js
const [first, setFirst] = signal("Ada");
const [last, setLast] = signal("Lovelace");
const fullName = computed(() => `${first()} ${last()}`);

effect(() => console.log(fullName())); // "Ada Lovelace"
setLast("Byron");                        // "Ada Byron"
js

Step 4: batching and the glitch problem

Our naive implementation has a flaw. Look at this "diamond" graph:

const [a, setA] = signal(1);
const b = computed(() => a() * 2);
const c = computed(() => a() + 1);

effect(() => console.log(b(), c()));
setA(2);
js

The effect depends on a twice (through b and c). With eager scheduling, it can run once after b is marked dirty and again after c — the first run might even see an inconsistent mix of old and new values. That intermediate state is called a glitch.

The fix used by real libraries is two-phase propagation: first mark everything downstream as stale, then run effects once, after the write completes. A simple version uses a queue and a batch depth:

let batchDepth = 0;
const pendingEffects = new Set();

export function batch(fn) {
  batchDepth++;
  try {
    fn();
  } finally {
    batchDepth--;
    if (batchDepth === 0) flush();
  }
}

function flush() {
  for (const run of [...pendingEffects]) {
    pendingEffects.delete(run);
    run();
  }
}
js

Then change the effect's schedule to enqueue instead of running immediately, and have write wrap its notifications in batch:

schedule() {
  pendingEffects.add(run);
},

// inside signal's write():
batch(() => {
  for (const sub of [...subscribers]) sub.schedule();
});
js

Now the diamond logs 4 3 exactly once. Because computed values are lazy and only recompute when read, the effect always sees a consistent snapshot. Production libraries go further, tracking per-node versions or colours ("clean / check / dirty") so that a computed whose inputs changed but whose output didn't stops propagation early.

View this part on the site

How this maps to real frameworks

Concept Our version Solid Preact Signals Vue
Source signal() createSignal signal ref
Derived computed() createMemo computed computed
Side effect effect() createEffect effect watchEffect
Batching batch() batch batch scheduler

The JSX compiler in Solid wraps each dynamic expression in an effect, which is why only the text node that reads a signal updates when it changes — components run exactly once.

Trade-offs worth knowing

  • Memory: every dependency edge is a Set entry. Large graphs need cleanup on disposal or they leak.
  • Debuggability: implicit tracking is convenient but can hide why something re-ran. Good devtools matter.
  • Equality: Object.is means mutating an object in place won't notify. Treat signal values as immutable, or use a custom equality function.

Conclusion

Signals come down to a global "current observer" pointer, sets of subscribers, lazy cached derivations and a scheduler that avoids glitches. With those four ideas you can read the source of Solid or Preact Signals and recognise every part, and you'll understand why the TC39 proposal aims to standardise exactly this core.
