  • SolidJS documentation
  • Proxy and Reflect
  • Hunting memory leaks

item.title: Hunting Memory Leaks in JavaScript Applications
item.description: How garbage collection really decides what to keep, the five leak patterns behind most SPA memory issues, and a repeatable DevTools workflow using heap snapshots, allocation timelines and WeakRef-aware design.
item.content:encoded:
Leaks in a garbage-collected language

JavaScript frees memory automatically, so how can it leak? Because the garbage collector only frees what is unreachable. A leak is memory that's still reachable from a root (the global object, the current call stack, active closures, DOM, timers) even though your program will never use it again.

In long-lived single-page apps — dashboards left open all day, editors, chat clients — these small mistakes add up until the tab gets slow or crashes.

How reachability works

Modern engines use a mark-and-sweep collector (generational and incremental in V8's case): starting from the roots, mark everything reachable by following references, then sweep everything unmarked.

let user = { name: "Ada" };
const admins = [user];

user = null;
// The object is still reachable through `admins[0]`, so it stays in memory.
js

To find a leak, you must find the retaining path: the chain of references from a root to the object that shouldn't be there anymore.

View this part on the site

The five usual suspects

1. Forgotten event listeners and subscriptions

function mountChart(el) {
  const chart = createHugeChart(el);
  window.addEventListener("resize", () => chart.resize()); // never removed
}
js

window lives forever, so it keeps the listener alive, the listener's closure keeps chart, and chart keeps its DOM node and data. Mount and unmount this ten times and you have ten charts in memory.

function mountChart(el) {
  const chart = createHugeChart(el);
  const controller = new AbortController();
  window.addEventListener("resize", () => chart.resize(), { signal: controller.signal });
  return () => {
    controller.abort(); // removes every listener registered with this signal
    chart.destroy();
  };
}
js

AbortController is the cleanest way to remove many listeners at once. In React, return the cleanup from useEffect.

2. Timers and intervals

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => poll(store), 5000);
  // ❌ no cleanup: the interval and everything its callback references live forever
}, []);

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => poll(store), 5000);
  return () => clearInterval(id); // ✅
}, []);
js

3. Detached DOM nodes

A DOM node removed from the document but still referenced from JavaScript can't be collected — and it keeps its whole subtree alive.

const cache = new Map();

function showRow(id) {
  const row = document.createElement("tr");
  cache.set(id, row);       // reference kept forever
  table.appendChild(row);
}

function clearTable() {
  table.innerHTML = "";     // rows are detached, but the Map still holds them
}
js

Heap snapshots let you filter for "Detached" nodes, which makes this pattern easy to spot.

4. Unbounded caches

Memoisation without eviction is a leak with a nice name:

const cache = {};
function getUserView(user) {
  return (cache[user.id] ??= renderExpensiveView(user)); // grows forever
}
js

Fix it with a size limit (LRU), a TTL, or by keying on objects with a WeakMap:

const cache = new WeakMap();
function getUserView(user) {
  let view = cache.get(user);
  if (!view) cache.set(user, (view = renderExpensiveView(user)));
  return view;
}
// When `user` becomes unreachable elsewhere, the cache entry can be collected too.
js

5. Closures capturing more than you think

Closures created in the same scope can share a context object in V8. A long-lived closure can therefore keep alive a large variable that only a short-lived sibling closure used:

function setup() {
  const hugeData = new Array(1e6).fill("x");
  const unused = () => hugeData.length;  // references hugeData
  return () => console.log("tick");      // may still retain hugeData via the shared context
}
const tick = setup();
js

If a heap snapshot shows a large object retained by a context of a function that doesn't use it, this is why. The fix is to avoid capturing big values in scopes that also create long-lived callbacks, or to set them to null when done.

A repeatable DevTools workflow

Step 1: confirm there is a leak

Open Performance monitor (Command menu → "Show Performance monitor") and watch JS heap size and DOM Nodes while repeating an action — open and close a modal 20 times, navigate between two routes, and so on. Force GC with the trash-can button in the Memory panel. If the baseline keeps climbing after GC, something is leaking.

Step 2: three-snapshot technique

  1. Load the page, do the action once (to warm caches), force GC, take Snapshot 1.
  2. Repeat the action several times, force GC, take Snapshot 2.
  3. Repeat again, force GC, take Snapshot 3.
  4. In Snapshot 3, choose "Objects allocated between Snapshot 1 and Snapshot 2".

Objects created during the middle phase that survive into snapshot 3 are your strongest leak candidates. Sort by Retained Size, not Shallow Size — retained size is how much memory would be freed if that object were collected.

Step 3: read the retainers

Select a suspicious object and read the Retainers panel from bottom to top. You'll see something like:

ChartInstance
  ← chart in system / Context
  ← context in () @ chart.js:14
  ← [3] in Array (event listeners)
  ← resize in Window
text

That's the leak: the resize listener on window, created at chart.js:14.

Step 4: allocation timeline for the tricky cases

The Allocations on timeline profile records allocations as blue bars over time; bars that stay blue (rather than turning grey) were never freed. Click one to see the allocation stack trace.

WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry

WeakRef holds a reference that doesn't prevent collection, and FinalizationRegistry runs a callback some time after an object is collected:

const registry = new FinalizationRegistry((key) => {
  console.log(`${key} was garbage-collected`);
});
registry.register(chartInstance, "chart#1");
js

They're useful for caches of expensive, recreatable objects and for verifying fixes during development. But GC timing is non-deterministic and finalizers may never run, so don't use them for program logic or essential cleanup.

Preventing leaks by design

  • Every add has a matching remove: listeners, intervals, observers (ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver), subscriptions and WebSockets.
  • Tie lifetimes to a single AbortSignal per component or feature.
  • Bound every cache. Prefer WeakMap when keys are objects.
  • Add a memory test to CI for critical flows: drive the UI with Playwright, read performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory() (it requires cross-origin isolation) or snapshot via the Chrome DevTools Protocol, and fail when growth passes a threshold.

Conclusion

Most leaks come from one of five patterns: listeners, timers, detached DOM, unbounded caches and over-capturing closures. Confirm the leak with the performance monitor, isolate it with the three-snapshot technique, and follow the retainer chain to the exact line. With cleanup tied to clear lifetimes, long-running apps stay fast after hours of use.

Further reading

  • Fix memory problems, Chrome DevTools
  • WeakRef on MDN
  • AbortController on MDN
  • Build signals from scratch
  • Web Workers in practice

item.title: Inside the JavaScript Event Loop: Tasks, Microtasks and the Rendering Steps
item.description: A precise mental model of how the browser schedules your code — tasks, microtasks, requestAnimationFrame and rendering — and how to use it to write UIs that never freeze.
item.content:encoded:
Why the event loop still trips up senior engineers

Most of us learned the event loop as "JavaScript is single-threaded, async things go into a queue". That model is good enough until it isn't: a Promise chain that starves the renderer, a setTimeout(fn, 0) that fires after a frame you expected it to beat, or a requestAnimationFrame callback that runs twice as often as you thought.

This article builds a precise model based on the HTML specification, then uses it to answer real production questions.

The model in one picture

Every browser tab's main thread runs a loop that, simplified, looks like this:

while (true) {
  // 1. Run ONE task (macrotask) from a task queue
  const task = pickTaskFromSomeQueue();
  if (task) run(task);

  // 2. Drain the ENTIRE microtask queue
  while (microtaskQueue.length) {
    run(microtaskQueue.shift());
  }

  // 3. Maybe render (roughly every 16.7ms on a 60Hz display)
  if (isRenderingOpportunity()) {
    runResizeAndScrollSteps();
    runAnimationFrameCallbacks(); // requestAnimationFrame
    recalcStyle();
    layout();
    runResizeObserverCallbacks();
    paint();
  }

  // 4. If idle, run requestIdleCallback callbacks
}
js

Three rules fall out of this pseudo-code, and nearly every event-loop puzzle reduces to them:

  1. One task per turn. Tasks never run back-to-back without giving microtasks (and possibly rendering) a chance.
  2. Microtasks drain completely. If a microtask schedules another microtask, that one runs too, before anything else.
  3. Rendering is opportunistic. The browser decides when a frame is due; your code can only ask to run right before it, via requestAnimationFrame.

View this part on the site

Tasks vs microtasks

Tasks (often called macrotasks) come from: setTimeout/setInterval, user input events, MessageChannel messages, network callbacks, and parsing HTML.

Microtasks come from: promise reactions (.then, await continuations), queueMicrotask, and MutationObserver.

Here's the classic quiz:

console.log("1: script");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2: timeout"), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("3: microtask A"))
  .then(() => console.log("4: microtask B"));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("5: queueMicrotask"));

console.log("6: script end");
js

Output:

1: script
6: script end
3: microtask A
5: queueMicrotask
4: microtask B
2: timeout
text

The whole script is itself a task. When it finishes, the microtask queue holds A and 5. Running A enqueues B at the end of the queue, so 5 goes first. Only after the queue is empty does the loop pick the next task — the timeout.

View this part on the site

await is just a microtask boundary

Every await splits a function: everything after it becomes a promise reaction. This is why async code that "looks" synchronous can still interleave with other microtasks:

async function a() {
  console.log("a1");
  await null;
  console.log("a2");
}

async function b() {
  console.log("b1");
  await null;
  console.log("b2");
}

a();
b();
// a1, b1, a2, b2
js

Rule of thumb: an await never yields to rendering or to user input. It only yields to other microtasks. If you want the browser to paint, you need a task boundary or a frame boundary.

Starving the renderer with microtasks

Because microtasks drain completely, a recursive microtask chain blocks the page exactly like an infinite while loop:

function spin() {
  queueMicrotask(spin); // the page is now frozen
}
spin();
js

A more realistic version: processing a big array with await in a loop and expecting the UI to stay responsive.

// ❌ Looks async, still blocks painting until all 50k items are done
async function processAll(items) {
  for (const item of items) {
    await processItem(item); // resolves synchronously → microtask
  }
}
js

If processItem resolves immediately, every iteration is a microtask and the browser never gets a rendering opportunity.

Yielding to the main thread properly

To let the browser paint and handle input, yield with a task, not a microtask. The modern API is scheduler.yield(), with a setTimeout fallback:

function yieldToMain() {
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) {
    return scheduler.yield();
  }
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

async function processAll(items) {
  let lastYield = performance.now();
  for (const item of items) {
    processItem(item);
    // Yield roughly every 50ms (the "long task" threshold)
    if (performance.now() - lastYield > 50) {
      await yieldToMain();
      lastYield = performance.now();
    }
  }
}
js

Yielding makes a frame possible. It doesn't force one, so when something must be visible before the work starts, wait for a frame explicitly. The INP article has a demo of the difference.

scheduler.yield() has a nice property over setTimeout: the continuation is placed at the front of the task queue, so your work resumes before other, lower-priority tasks that were queued in the meantime.

Where requestAnimationFrame fits

rAF callbacks run in the rendering step, right before style and layout. That makes it the right place for visual updates and the wrong place for heavy computation.

// Measuring before the browser has applied a change
el.classList.add("expanded");

requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  // Still before layout for this frame. Reading layout here forces it.
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    // Runs in the *next* frame — the previous one has been painted.
    el.classList.add("animate");
  });
});
js

The "double rAF" trick is a well-known way to guarantee a style has been committed to a frame before you change it again, which is needed to trigger CSS transitions from an initial state.

Two other facts worth knowing:

  • rAF is paused in background tabs. Don't use it for logic that must keep running.
  • rAF fires at the display's refresh rate. On a 120Hz screen, a rAF-driven animation that assumes 16.7ms per frame will run twice as fast. Always use the timestamp argument to compute deltas.
let last;
function tick(now) {
  const dt = last === undefined ? 0 : (now - last) / 1000; // seconds
  last = now;
  position += velocity * dt; // frame-rate independent
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}
requestAnimationFrame(tick);
js

setTimeout(fn, 0) is not zero

Timers are clamped: after 5 levels of nesting, browsers enforce a minimum of about 4ms, and in background tabs timers can be throttled to once per second or less. If you need "as soon as possible, but after rendering and input", MessageChannel is the classic zero-delay task primitive (React's scheduler used it for years):

const channel = new MessageChannel();
const queue = [];
channel.port1.onmessage = () => queue.shift()?.();

function postTask(fn) {
  queue.push(fn);
  channel.port2.postMessage(null);
}
js

A debugging checklist

When something runs in the "wrong" order, ask:

  1. Is it a task or a microtask? Promise reactions always beat timers.
  2. Did the microtask queue drain? A long chain of thens delays everything else, including paint.
  3. Do I need a frame or a task? Visual changes belong in rAF; yielding for responsiveness needs a task (scheduler.yield, setTimeout, MessageChannel).
  4. Is the tab in the background? rAF stops and timers are throttled.

Conclusion

Learn the loop as three rules — one task per turn, microtasks drain fully, rendering is opportunistic — and most "weird async bugs" become predictable. That predictability is what lets you break long work into chunks, keep Interaction to Next Paint low, and write animations that stay smooth on every refresh rate.

Further reading

  • Event loops in the HTML Standard
  • Scheduler.yield() on MDN
  • Optimize long tasks on web.dev
  • Taming INP
  • The browser rendering pipeline

item.title: Metaprogramming in JavaScript with Proxy and Reflect
item.description: Intercept property access, validation, and function calls with Proxy traps. Learn the invariants, the role of Reflect and receivers, and build a tiny reactive store, a validation layer and a negative-index array.
item.content:encoded:
What a Proxy actually is

A Proxy wraps a target object and lets you intercept the internal operations the engine performs on it — [[Get]], [[Set]], [[HasProperty]], [[Delete]], [[OwnPropertyKeys]], [[Call]] and more. Each interceptable operation is a trap on the handler object.

const target = { greeting: "hello" };

const proxy = new Proxy(target, {
  get(target, key, receiver) {
    console.log(`read ${String(key)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);
  },
});

proxy.greeting; // logs "read greeting", returns "hello"
js

That's the whole API surface. The interesting part is using it correctly.

View this part on the site

Why you should always forward with Reflect

Reflect has one method per trap with the exact same signature. It performs the default behaviour. Using it instead of target[key] matters because of the receiver argument:

const base = {
  _name: "base",
  get name() {
    return this._name;
  },
};

const proxy = new Proxy(base, {
  get(target, key, receiver) {
    return target[key]; // ❌ the getter runs with this === target
  },
});

const child = Object.create(proxy);
child._name = "child";
child.name; // "base" — wrong!
js

When child.name walks up the prototype chain into the proxy, receiver is child. target[key] drops it and calls the getter on target. Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) preserves this === child and returns "child". The same applies to set and setters.

Trap invariants: what you cannot lie about

Proxies can't violate certain invariants of the target, or the engine throws a TypeError. For example:

  • get must return the actual value for a non-writable, non-configurable data property.
  • has can't hide a non-configurable property.
  • ownKeys must include all non-configurable own keys, and must not add keys if the target is non-extensible.
const frozen = Object.freeze({ x: 1 });
const liar = new Proxy(frozen, { get: () => 42 });
liar.x; // TypeError: 'get' on proxy: property 'x' is a read-only and
        // non-configurable data property ... but the proxy did not return its actual value
js

These invariants exist so that security guarantees like Object.freeze can't be undermined by a proxy.

Example 1: negative array indices

function withNegativeIndices(array) {
  return new Proxy(array, {
    get(target, key, receiver) {
      if (typeof key === "string" && /^-\d+$/.test(key)) {
        key = String(target.length + Number(key));
      }
      return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);
    },
  });
}

const list = withNegativeIndices(["a", "b", "c"]);
list[-1]; // "c"
list.at(-2); // "b" — all normal methods still work
js

Note that property keys always arrive as strings or symbols, never numbers — list[-1] reaches the trap as "-1".

Example 2: a validation layer

function typed(schema) {
  return new Proxy({}, {
    set(target, key, value, receiver) {
      const expected = schema[key];
      if (!expected) {
        throw new TypeError(`Unknown field "${String(key)}"`);
      }
      if (typeof value !== expected) {
        throw new TypeError(`"${String(key)}" must be ${expected}, got ${typeof value}`);
      }
      return Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver);
    },
  });
}

const user = typed({ name: "string", age: "number" });
user.name = "Ada";
user.age = "36"; // TypeError: "age" must be number, got string
js

The set trap must return true on success. Returning false throws a TypeError in strict mode — which is what modules and classes always are.

Example 3: a tiny reactive store (how Vue 3 works)

Vue 3's reactivity is built on proxies. Here's the core idea in a few lines:

const targetMap = new WeakMap(); // target -> key -> Set<effect>
let activeEffect = null;

function track(target, key) {
  if (!activeEffect) return;
  let deps = targetMap.get(target);
  if (!deps) targetMap.set(target, (deps = new Map()));
  let set = deps.get(key);
  if (!set) deps.set(key, (set = new Set()));
  set.add(activeEffect);
}

function trigger(target, key) {
  targetMap.get(target)?.get(key)?.forEach((fn) => fn());
}

export function reactive(obj) {
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    get(target, key, receiver) {
      track(target, key);
      const value = Reflect.get(target, key, receiver);
      // Lazily make nested objects reactive
      return value !== null && typeof value === "object" ? reactive(value) : value;
    },
    set(target, key, value, receiver) {
      const old = target[key];
      const ok = Reflect.set(target, key, value, receiver);
      if (ok && !Object.is(old, value)) trigger(target, key);
      return ok;
    },
  });
}

export function watchEffect(fn) {
  const run = () => {
    activeEffect = run;
    try { fn(); } finally { activeEffect = null; }
  };
  run();
}
js
const state = reactive({ user: { name: "Ada" } });
watchEffect(() => console.log(state.user.name));
state.user.name = "Grace"; // logs "Grace"
js

Using a WeakMap keyed by the raw target means dependency data is garbage-collected with the object. A production version also caches proxies per target (so reactive(obj) === reactive(obj)), and handles arrays, Map/Set, and has/ownKeys traps for in and iteration.

Revocable proxies for capability security

Proxy.revocable returns a proxy plus a revoke function. After revoking, every operation on the proxy throws. That's useful for handing a third-party plugin temporary access:

const { proxy: api, revoke } = Proxy.revocable(internalApi, {});
plugin.init(api);
// later...
revoke(); // the plugin can no longer touch internalApi through `api`
js

Performance and pitfalls

  • Proxies are slower than plain property access because traps defeat many engine optimisations (inline caches). Don't put them in hot inner loops.
  • Identity: proxy !== target. Code that uses objects as Map keys or does === checks can break.
  • Private fields don't work through proxies. #field access checks the actual object, and the proxy isn't the instance:
class Counter {
  #count = 0;
  inc() { return ++this.#count; }
}
const p = new Proxy(new Counter(), {});
p.inc(); // TypeError: Cannot read private member #count
js

Fix it by binding methods to the target in the get trap when the value is a function.

  • Built-ins with internal slots (Map, Set, Date, typed arrays) have the same problem — their methods need this to be the real object.

Conclusion

Use Reflect to forward every trap with its receiver, respect the invariants, and keep proxies out of hot paths. Follow those rules and proxies give you validation layers, observable state, API versioning shims and sandboxing without changing the code that uses the object.

Further reading

  • Proxy on MDN
  • Reflect on MDN
  • Vue: Reactivity in depth
  • Build signals from scratch

item.title: A Mental Model for React Server Components and Streaming
item.description: Server Components, Client Components, the RSC payload, Suspense streaming and Server Actions — explained as one coherent model, with the composition patterns and pitfalls that matter in a real Next.js codebase.
item.content:encoded:
Two kinds of components, one tree

React Server Components (RSC) split your component tree across two environments:

  • Server Components run only on the server (at build time or request time). They can be async, read databases and files directly, and ship zero JavaScript to the browser.
  • Client Components are the components you already know. They are marked with "use client", run on the server for the initial HTML and in the browser, and can use state, effects and event handlers.

In the Next.js App Router, every component is a Server Component unless something makes it a client one.

// app/posts/page.tsx — a Server Component
import { db } from "@/lib/db";
import { LikeButton } from "./like-button";

export default async function PostsPage() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany({ take: 20 }); // direct data access

  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map((post) => (
        <li key={post.id}>
          <h2>{post.title}</h2>
          <LikeButton postId={post.id} initialLikes={post.likes} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
tsx
// app/posts/like-button.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";

export function LikeButton({ postId, initialLikes }: { postId: string; initialLikes: number }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(initialLikes);
  return <button onClick={() => setLikes((n) => n + 1)}>♥ {likes}</button>;
}
tsx

The database client, the query and the mapping code never reach the browser. Only LikeButton's code does.

View this part on the site

"use client" marks a boundary, not a component

The directive marks a module boundary: that file and everything it imports become part of the client bundle. That's why you should push "use client" as far down the tree as possible — mark the small interactive leaf, not the whole page.

A frequent mistake is putting "use client" at the top of a layout because one child needs useState. Now every import of that layout — markdown parsers, date libraries, icon sets — ships to the browser.

What actually goes over the wire

Server Components don't render to HTML in the browser; they render to the RSC payload, a streamable serialised description of the tree. Conceptually it looks like:

0: ["$", "ul", null, { children: ["$L1", "$L2"] }]
1: ["$", "li", null, { children: [["$", "h2", null, { children: "Hello RSC" }],
     ["$", "$Lclient:LikeButton", null, { postId: "1", initialLikes: 3 }]] }]
client:LikeButton: { id: "./like-button.js", chunks: ["chunk-abc.js"] }
text

Server Component output is inlined as plain elements. Client Components appear as references to a module plus the props to pass them. The browser downloads only those referenced chunks and hydrates them.

Two consequences follow:

  1. Props passed from server to client must be serialisable — plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, Date, Map, Set, promises and server actions. Not class instances, and not ordinary functions.
  2. Navigations fetch payloads, not HTML. On client navigation, React requests the RSC payload for the new route and merges it into the existing tree, so client state in shared layouts survives.

The composition rule: pass Server Components as children

A Client Component can't import a Server Component (the import would pull server-only code into the client bundle). But it can render one passed in as a prop:

// ❌ Inside a client component file
import { ServerSidebar } from "./server-sidebar"; // becomes client code

// ✅ Compose from a server component instead
// app/layout.tsx (server)
<CollapsiblePanel>          {/* client: owns open/closed state */}
  <ServerSidebar />          {/* server: rendered on the server, passed as children */}
</CollapsiblePanel>
tsx

children here is already-rendered output in the RSC payload, so the client component just places it. This "donut" pattern — an interactive shell around server-rendered content — is the most important RSC composition technique.

Streaming with Suspense

Because the payload is a stream, the server can send the page shell immediately and fill in slow parts later:

import { Suspense } from "react";

export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />                                  {/* sent immediately */}
      <Suspense fallback={<ChartSkeleton />}>
        <RevenueChart />                          {/* async; streams in when ready */}
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
        <ActivityFeed />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}
tsx

Each boundary resolves independently. The user sees and can interact with the header while the chart query is still running, and React hydrates parts of the page as their code arrives (selective hydration), prioritising the part the user interacts with first.

Watch out for waterfalls. Awaiting in sequence serialises requests:

// ❌ 300ms + 300ms
const user = await getUser(id);
const orders = await getOrders(id);

// ✅ ~300ms — start both, then await
const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getOrders(id)]);
tsx

Or better, move each fetch into the component that needs it and give each its own Suspense boundary.

Mutations with Server Actions

Server Actions are async functions marked with "use server" that the client can call like a function. React turns the call into a POST request:

// app/posts/actions.ts
"use server";

import { revalidatePath } from "next/cache";

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  const title = String(formData.get("title") ?? "");
  if (!title) return { error: "Title is required" };
  await db.post.create({ data: { title } });
  revalidatePath("/posts"); // re-render affected server components
}
tsx
// Works even before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement)
<form action={createPost}>
  <input name="title" />
  <button type="submit">Publish</button>
</form>
tsx

Treat every Server Action as a public API endpoint. Anyone can call it with any arguments. Authenticate, authorise and validate inside the action itself — never rely on the UI hiding a button.

Pitfalls checklist

  • Leaking secrets: a module imported by a client component can end up in the browser. Add import "server-only" to modules that touch secrets so the build fails if that happens.
  • Context: createContext providers must be Client Components. Wrap them in a small client Providers component and render it from your server layout.
  • Over-fetching in loops: use React's cache() to dedupe the same data request across components within a single render.
  • Large props: everything you pass to a client component is serialised into the payload. Pass the 3 fields it needs, not the full database row.

Conclusion

Server Components render to a serialisable stream. Client Components are references in that stream that hydrate in the browser. "use client" marks a bundle boundary, and composition through children lets server content live inside interactive shells. Suspense streams the slow parts, and Server Actions handle mutations as public endpoints. Keep "use client" at the leaves, fetch in parallel and validate every action, and RSC will give you smaller bundles and faster pages.

  • Shipping a static Next.js site
  • React architecture

item.title: Taming INP: A Practical Guide to Interaction to Next Paint
item.description: INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital. Learn how it's measured, how to find the slow interactions in your app, and the concrete techniques that cut it: yielding, deferring non-urgent work, React transitions and smaller DOMs.
item.content:encoded:
What INP measures

Interaction to Next Paint observes every click, tap and key press during a page visit and reports (roughly) the worst one — the 98th percentile for pages with many interactions. Each interaction's latency is the time from the input until the browser paints the next frame after handling it.

That latency has three parts:

  1. Input delay — the main thread was busy with something else when the user interacted.
  2. Processing time — your event handlers ran.
  3. Presentation delay — style, layout, paint and compositing for the resulting frame.

Thresholds: ≤ 200ms is good, > 500ms is poor, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads.

Because INP covers the whole visit and not just the first input, it punishes exactly the things heavy single-page apps do: big re-renders, synchronous state updates and long tasks during hydration.

View this part on the site

Step 1: measure in the field

Lab tools can't know which interactions real users perform. Collect field data with the web-vitals library and the attribution build:

import { onINP } from "web-vitals/attribution";

onINP(({ value, rating, attribution }) => {
  navigator.sendBeacon("/analytics", JSON.stringify({
    value,
    rating,
    target: attribution.interactionTarget,       // CSS selector of the element
    type: attribution.interactionType,           // "pointer" | "keyboard"
    inputDelay: attribution.inputDelay,
    processing: attribution.processingDuration,
    presentation: attribution.presentationDelay,
    // Long Animation Frame entries explain *which scripts* were responsible
    scripts: attribution.longAnimationFrameEntries
      ?.flatMap((e) => e.scripts.map((s) => s.sourceURL)),
  }));
});
js

The breakdown tells you where to look:

Dominant phase Usual cause Fix
Input delay Long tasks already running (hydration, timers, third-party scripts) Break up long tasks, defer third parties
Processing Expensive handlers, large synchronous re-renders Yield, defer, memoise, transitions
Presentation Huge DOM, layout thrashing, expensive CSS Smaller DOM, content-visibility, avoid forced layouts

Step 2: do the visible work first, defer the rest

The single most effective pattern: in the handler, do only what's needed for the next frame, then yield before the rest.

// Yield with a *task*, so the browser can paint and handle input
function yieldToMain() {
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) return scheduler.yield();
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

// Runs in a new task after the next frame
function nextFrame() {
  return new Promise((resolve) => requestAnimationFrame(() => setTimeout(resolve, 0)));
}

button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  // 1. Immediate visual feedback
  button.classList.add("is-loading");

  // 2. Wait until that feedback has been painted
  await nextFrame();

  // 3. Non-urgent work happens after the paint
  recalculateRecommendations();
  sendAnalytics("click");
});
js

Why not just yieldToMain() in step 2? Because yielding allows a frame without guaranteeing one. Continuations from scheduler.yield() run with priority, and the browser may resume your work before it paints. When I built the demo below with yields alone, the next frame arrived only after all the work was done. Wait for the frame first, then yield to keep input responsive.

Analytics, logging and prefetching almost never need to block the frame. Move them behind a yield or into requestIdleCallback.

Step 3: break up long tasks

Any task over 50ms is a long task. If one is running when the user clicks, the click has to wait. Chunk heavy loops:

async function filterLargeList(items, predicate) {
  const result = [];
  let deadline = performance.now() + 8; // ~half a frame
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    if (predicate(items[i])) result.push(items[i]);
    if (performance.now() > deadline) {
      await yieldToMain();
      deadline = performance.now() + 8;
    }
  }
  return result;
}
js

If the work is pure computation (parsing, sorting, diffing), move it off the main thread entirely into a Web Worker.

View this part on the site

Step 4: React-specific techniques

React 18+ gives you concurrent rendering that can be interrupted by input:

import { useState, useTransition, useDeferredValue } from "react";

function Search({ items }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("");

  return (
    <>
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={(e) => {
          setQuery(e.target.value);                       // urgent: keep typing snappy
          startTransition(() => setFilter(e.target.value)); // can be interrupted
        }}
      />
      {isPending && <Spinner />}
      <Results items={items} filter={filter} />
    </>
  );
}
jsx

The input update commits immediately; the expensive results render happens in a transition that React abandons and restarts if another keystroke arrives. useDeferredValue achieves the same thing when you don't control the state setter.

Other React wins:

  • Memoise expensive subtrees (memo, or the React Compiler) so a keystroke doesn't re-render the world.
  • Virtualise long lists — rendering 5,000 rows is slow no matter how fast each row is.
  • Avoid hydration-time long tasks with selective hydration (Suspense boundaries) and by shipping less client JavaScript (Server Components).

Step 5: reduce presentation delay

Even with a fast handler, the frame can be slow to produce:

  • Large DOMs make style recalculation and layout expensive. Keep it under a few thousand nodes where possible.
  • content-visibility: auto lets the browser skip rendering off-screen sections:
.feed-item {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 320px; /* placeholder size to avoid scroll jumps */
}
css
  • Avoid layout thrashing — interleaving DOM writes and layout reads in a loop forces synchronous layout each iteration:
// ❌ read → write → read → write: forced layout each time
for (const el of cards) el.style.height = el.offsetWidth * 0.5 + "px";

// ✅ batch reads, then batch writes
const widths = cards.map((el) => el.offsetWidth);
cards.forEach((el, i) => (el.style.height = widths[i] * 0.5 + "px"));
js

A debugging workflow that works

  1. Find the worst interactions from field data (target selector + phase breakdown).
  2. Reproduce in Chrome DevTools' Performance panel with CPU throttling at 4× or 6×.
  3. Look at the Interactions track; expand the long interaction and read the flame chart under it.
  4. Apply the matching fix from the table above, then verify in the field — lab improvements don't always transfer.

Conclusion

INP rewards apps that respond first and compute later. Show feedback in the next frame, yield before non-urgent work, keep long tasks off the main thread, and let React's transitions keep input urgent. These habits fix a metric and also make the app feel faster.

Further reading

  • Interaction to Next Paint on web.dev
  • web-vitals library
  • useTransition in the React docs
  • Inside the JavaScript event loop
  • A front-end performance workflow

item.title: Type-Level Programming in TypeScript: Conditional, Mapped and Template Literal Types
item.description: Treat TypeScript's type system as a small functional language. Learn conditional types and infer, distributive behaviour, key remapping, recursive types and template literals, then build a type-safe router and a deep-path getter.
item.content:encoded:
Types are a programming language

TypeScript's type system is Turing-complete, which in practice means you can compute types from other types. Once you see it as a small functional language — with functions (generic types), conditionals (conditional types), loops (recursion and mapped types) and string manipulation (template literal types) — advanced library types stop looking like magic.

Generic types are functions

type Box<T> = { value: T };       // a function from T to a type
type StringBox = Box<string>;     // calling it
ts

Conditional types are if statements

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

type A = IsString<"hi">; // true
type B = IsString<42>;   // false
ts

extends here means "is assignable to". Combined with infer, conditional types also do pattern matching — they can pull pieces out of a type:

type ElementType<T> = T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type Awaited2<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? Awaited2<U> : T;
type ReturnOf<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;

type E = ElementType<string[]>;            // string
type P = Awaited2<Promise<Promise<number>>>; // number (recursion!)
ts

The distributive surprise

When the checked type is a naked type parameter and you pass a union, the conditional is applied to each member separately:

type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type X = ToArray<string | number>; // string[] | number[]  (not (string | number)[])
ts

That's usually what you want (it's how Exclude and Extract work), but sometimes it isn't. Wrap both sides in a tuple to turn distribution off:

type ToArrayNonDist<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never;
type Y = ToArrayNonDist<string | number>; // (string | number)[]
ts

The same trick gives a reliable IsNever check, because never is an empty union and distributing over it yields never:

type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
ts

Mapped types are loops over keys

type ReadonlyDeep<T> = {
  readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? ReadonlyDeep<T[K]> : T[K];
};
ts

Since TypeScript 4.1, the as clause lets you rename or filter keys while mapping:

type Getters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K];
};

type User = { name: string; age: number };
type UserGetters = Getters<User>;
// { getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }

// Filtering: returning `never` from `as` removes the key
type OnlyFunctions<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends (...args: any[]) => any ? K : never]: T[K];
};
ts

Template literal types are string functions

Template literal types concatenate and — with infer — parse strings at the type level:

type Split<S extends string, D extends string> =
  S extends `${infer Head}${D}${infer Tail}`
    ? [Head, ...Split<Tail, D>]
    : [S];

type Parts = Split<"a.b.c", ".">; // ["a", "b", "c"]
ts

View this part on the site

Project 1: a type-safe router

Let's extract route parameters from a path string, so params is fully typed:

type ExtractParams<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? { [K in Param | keyof ExtractParams<`/${Rest}`>]: string }
    : Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? { [K in Param]: string }
      : {};

function route<P extends string>(
  path: P,
  handler: (params: ExtractParams<P>) => void
) {
  /* register the route */
}

route("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", (params) => {
  params.userId; // string ✅
  params.postId; // string ✅
  params.foo;    // ❌ Property 'foo' does not exist
});
ts

The type recursively peels off :param/ segments and merges the found names into one object type. This is the same technique used by typed routers such as those in Hono and TanStack Router.

Project 2: a typed deep get

type Paths<T> = T extends object
  ? {
      [K in keyof T & string]: T[K] extends object
        ? K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}`
        : K;
    }[keyof T & string]
  : never;

type PathValue<T, P extends string> =
  P extends `${infer K}.${infer Rest}`
    ? K extends keyof T
      ? PathValue<T[K], Rest>
      : never
    : P extends keyof T
      ? T[P]
      : never;

function get<T, P extends Paths<T>>(obj: T, path: P): PathValue<T, P> {
  return path.split(".").reduce<any>((acc, key) => acc?.[key], obj);
}

const config = { server: { port: 8080, tls: { enabled: true } } };

get(config, "server.port");        // number
get(config, "server.tls.enabled"); // boolean
get(config, "server.host");        // ❌ not assignable to the allowed paths
ts

The { ... }[keyof T] pattern at the end of Paths is a common idiom: build an object type whose values are what you want, then index it with all its keys to get a union of the values.

Keeping the compiler happy

Type-level code has real costs:

  • Recursion limits. TypeScript caps instantiation depth (about 50 for non-tail recursion, and up to 1,000 for tail-recursive conditional types). Write recursive types in tail position by passing an accumulator:
type Join<T extends string[], D extends string, Acc extends string = ""> =
  T extends [infer H extends string, ...infer R extends string[]]
    ? Join<R, D, Acc extends "" ? H : `${Acc}${D}${H}`>
    : Acc;

type J = Join<["a", "b", "c"], "-">; // "a-b-c"
ts
  • Editor performance. Deep types on hot paths slow down IntelliSense for everyone. Check with tsc --extendedDiagnostics and --generateTrace.
  • Readability. Name intermediate types and add a short comment explaining what the type computes. Future you will need it.

Conclusion

Conditional types are branching, infer is pattern matching, mapped types are loops, and template literals are string processing. Use them at the edges of your system — routers, API clients, form libraries, config loaders — where a strong type stops whole categories of bugs, and keep everyday application types simple.

Further reading

  • Creating types from types, TypeScript handbook
  • type-challenges
  • Never trust JSON.parse in a render

item.title: Off the Main Thread: Web Workers, Transferables and RPC in Practice
item.description: Move expensive work off the UI thread. Covers dedicated workers in modern bundlers, structured clone costs, zero-copy transferables, a promise-based RPC layer, SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics, and OffscreenCanvas.
item.content:encoded:
The main thread is shared and busy

Everything that makes your UI responsive — input handling, React rendering, style, layout, paint — competes for one thread. Every millisecond spent parsing a large JSON payload, filtering 100k rows or resizing an image on that thread is a millisecond the user's click has to wait.

Web Workers give you real OS threads with their own event loops. They can't touch the DOM, which is exactly why they're safe to run in parallel.

View this part on the site

Creating a worker with a modern bundler

Vite, webpack 5, Turbopack and Parcel all recognise this pattern and bundle the worker file for you:

// main.js
const worker = new Worker(new URL("./search.worker.js", import.meta.url), {
  type: "module",
});

worker.postMessage({ type: "index", docs });
worker.onmessage = (event) => {
  console.log("results", event.data);
};
js
// search.worker.js
let index;

self.onmessage = (event) => {
  const { type, docs, query } = event.data;
  if (type === "index") index = buildIndex(docs);
  if (type === "search") self.postMessage(search(index, query));
};
js

type: "module" lets the worker use import statements — supported in all modern browsers.

The hidden cost: structured clone

postMessage copies data with the structured clone algorithm. It handles Map, Set, Date, typed arrays, cyclic references and more, but it's a deep copy — performed synchronously on the sending thread.

Sending a 50MB object to a worker can itself block the main thread for tens of milliseconds. Measure before assuming a worker is a win, and design messages to be small:

  • send IDs or diffs instead of whole datasets,
  • keep large state inside the worker and query it,
  • or transfer instead of copying.

Zero-copy with transferables

Some objects — ArrayBuffer, MessagePort, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas, streams — can be transferred: ownership moves to the other thread without copying, and the sender's reference becomes unusable.

const pixels = new Uint8ClampedArray(width * height * 4);

worker.postMessage({ pixels }, [pixels.buffer]); // transfer list

console.log(pixels.byteLength); // 0 — the buffer is now "detached"
js

For binary data — images, audio, geometry, parsed file contents — transfer turns an O(n) copy into a constant-time handoff.

A promise-based RPC layer

Raw onmessage handlers get messy fast. Wrap them in a request/response protocol with IDs so calls look like async functions. This is the idea behind the popular Comlink library:

// rpc.js — shared by both sides
export function expose(api, endpoint = self) {
  endpoint.addEventListener("message", async (event) => {
    const { id, method, args } = event.data;
    try {
      const result = await api[method](...args);
      endpoint.postMessage({ id, result });
    } catch (error) {
      endpoint.postMessage({ id, error: { message: error.message, stack: error.stack } });
    }
  });
}

export function wrap(worker) {
  let nextId = 0;
  const pending = new Map();

  worker.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
    const { id, result, error } = event.data;
    const call = pending.get(id);
    if (!call) return;
    pending.delete(id);
    error ? call.reject(Object.assign(new Error(error.message), error)) : call.resolve(result);
  });

  return new Proxy({}, {
    get: (_, method) => (...args) =>
      new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        const id = nextId++;
        pending.set(id, { resolve, reject });
        worker.postMessage({ id, method, args });
      }),
  });
}
js
// image.worker.js
import { expose } from "./rpc.js";
expose({
  async blur(bitmap, radius) { /* ... */ },
  async parseCsv(text) { /* ... */ },
});

// main.js
import { wrap } from "./rpc.js";
const api = wrap(new Worker(new URL("./image.worker.js", import.meta.url), { type: "module" }));
const rows = await api.parseCsv(fileText); // looks local, runs in parallel
js

Using workers from React

Create the worker once, and terminate it on unmount:

function useWorker(factory) {
  const ref = useRef(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    const worker = factory();
    ref.current = wrap(worker);
    return () => worker.terminate();
  }, []);
  return ref;
}
jsx

Combine it with useTransition or a loading state so the UI stays interactive while the worker computes.

Shared memory: SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics

When copying or transferring isn't enough — for example, a physics simulation that both threads read every frame — SharedArrayBuffer gives both threads the same memory.

It requires the page to be cross-origin isolated, which means serving two headers:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
text

Shared memory brings data races, so use Atomics for coordination:

// main.js
const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(4);
const flag = new Int32Array(shared);
worker.postMessage({ shared });

// worker.js
self.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  const flag = new Int32Array(data.shared);
  doWork();
  Atomics.store(flag, 0, 1);
  Atomics.notify(flag, 0); // wake anyone waiting on index 0
};
js

Atomics.wait blocks a thread and isn't allowed on the main thread; use Atomics.waitAsync there instead, where supported.

OffscreenCanvas: rendering in a worker

Charts, maps and visualisations can render entirely off the main thread:

// main.js
const canvas = document.querySelector("canvas");
const offscreen = canvas.transferControlToOffscreen();
worker.postMessage({ canvas: offscreen }, [offscreen]);

// render.worker.js
self.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  const ctx = data.canvas.getContext("2d");
  function frame(t) {
    draw(ctx, t);
    requestAnimationFrame(frame); // rAF is available in dedicated workers
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
};
js

The canvas keeps animating smoothly even when the main thread is busy with a heavy React render.

When not to use a worker

  • The work takes under ~10ms — messaging overhead and complexity aren't worth it.
  • The work needs the DOM or layout information.
  • The payload is huge and can't be transferred — the clone may cost more than the computation.

Conclusion

Workers are the only way to get real parallelism in the browser. Start with a plain dedicated worker behind a small RPC wrapper, transfer binary data instead of cloning it, keep heavy state on the worker side, and reach for SharedArrayBuffer or OffscreenCanvas only when profiling shows you need them.

Further reading

  • Web Workers API on MDN
  • Transferable objects on MDN
  • Comlink
  • Taming INP
  • Resumable uploads

item.title: Shipping a Static Next.js Site: Seven Things the Docs Won't Warn You About
item.description: Metadata that silently disappears, two root layouts, social images without extensions, icons paid for twice. Lessons from rebuilding this bilingual site with Next.js 16 and static export.
item.content:encoded:
The setup

This site is a Next.js 16 App Router project with output: "export". The build produces plain files for GitHub Pages: no server, no edge functions, no image optimizer. It has two languages, a blog and a set of case studies.

View this part on the site

Static export is a great fit for content sites. These are the things that surprised me.

1. Metadata is replaced, not merged

A layout sets a default social image. A page sets its own title for sharing:

export async function generateMetadata() {
  return {
    openGraph: { title: "My article", type: "article" },
  };
}
app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx

The page now has no image. Next.js merges metadata shallowly: the page's openGraph object replaces the layout's. The same goes for alternates, so one article-specific canonical URL also removed the RSS link from every article here. Nothing warns you, and the page looks perfect until someone shares it.

The inverse hurts too. Pages that don't set alternates inherit it. The blog index was telling search engines that its canonical URL was the homepage.

The fix is one function that builds complete metadata, used by every page:

export function pageMetadata({ locale, path, title, description, image }: Input): Metadata {
  const url = absoluteUrl(localePath(locale, path));
  return {
    title,
    description,
    alternates: { canonical: url, languages: alternatesFor(path), types: rssFor(locale) },
    openGraph: { title, description, url, images: [image] },
    twitter: { card: "summary_large_image", title, description, images: [image] },
  };
}
lib/seo.ts

2. Two languages want two root layouts

lang and dir belong on <html>, and only a root layout renders it. Route groups allow several:

app/
  (en)/layout.tsx        → <html lang="en" dir="ltr">
  (en)/blog/page.tsx     → /blog/
  (fa)/layout.tsx        → <html lang="fa" dir="rtl">
  (fa)/fa/blog/page.tsx  → /fa/blog/
text

Both layouts are five lines around a shared component. Two consequences to plan for:

  • Navigating between them is a full page load, so use a plain <a> for the language switch.
  • There is no single layout for the 404 page. You need global-not-found.tsx, which is behind a flag in Next.js 16.

3. Don't use opengraph-image.tsx with static export

The file convention produces a file called opengraph-image, without an extension. A static host picks the content type from the extension, so it can't know it's a PNG. A route handler gives you control over the name:

export const dynamic = "force-static";

export const generateStaticParams = () => posts.map((p) => ({ kind: "blog", file: `${p.slug}.png` }));

export async function GET(_: Request, { params }: Context) {
  const { file } = await params;
  return new ImageResponse(<Card post={find(file)} />, { width: 1200, height: 630 });
}
app/og/[kind]/[file]/route.tsx

4. Server components are paid for twice

A server component adds no JavaScript. Its output still travels twice: as HTML, and again inside the React payload that hydration needs.

For text that compresses well, it hardly matters. For inline SVG it does. About thirty brand icons pushed the homepage from 40 to 78 KB of compressed HTML. Moving them into one external sprite brought it back:

<svg aria-hidden width={16} height={16}>
  <use href="/brand-icons.svg#react" />
</svg>
tsx

5. Pass server-rendered nodes into client components

The blog index filters cards in the browser. That doesn't mean the cards must be client components. The server renders them, and the client decides which to show:

<BlogFilter
  items={posts.map((post) => ({
    search: post.title.toLowerCase(),
    card: <PostCard post={post} />, // rendered on the server
  }))}
/>
tsx

More on this in the mental model for server components.

6. Check what your bundler merges

I used next/font in both layouts, one font per language. The build merged their CSS into one chunk, and preloading works per chunk. Every English page preloaded the Persian fonts, and the other way around.

Nothing in the code looked wrong. The network panel showed it immediately. I ended up hosting the fonts myself, with an explicit preload per language. The longer version includes the wrong fix I tried first.

7. Test the output, not the app

With static export, the out folder is the product. So test that: serve it the way the host does, and check files directly.

test("sitemap lists existing canonical URLs only", () => {
  const urls = [...xml.matchAll(/<loc>([^<]+)<\/loc>/g)].map(([, url]) => url);
  expect(urls.sort()).toEqual(htmlFiles.map((f) => `${SITE}${f.path}`).sort());
});
tests/seo.spec.ts

Similar tests check that every internal link and anchor resolves, that each page has an existing social image, and that language links point back at each other. They run in seconds and need no browser.

What I would choose again

Static export, server components by default, a single metadata function, and tests on the output. The framework is good at this. The surprises all come from the same place: conventions do something on your behalf, and you only see the result in the build. Look at the build.

item.title: A Front-End Performance Workflow That Survives Real Users
item.description: Measure in the field, find the one metric that hurts, break it into parts, fix the largest part, and put a budget on it. A workflow for LCP, INP and CLS, with numbers from a real site.
item.content:encoded:
Why checklists don't help

"Compress images, split code, use a CDN" is true for every site and useful for none in particular. A list can't tell you which of its twenty items is slowing down your page. A workflow can.

Here is one, in five steps. The examples come from this site.

Step 1: know the three targets

Metric Question it answers Good Poor
LCP When does the main content appear? ≤ 2.5 s > 4 s
INP How fast does the page react? ≤ 200 ms > 500 ms
CLS Does the layout jump? ≤ 0.1 > 0.25

They're judged at the 75th percentile of real visits. INP replaced First Input Delay in March 2024, so advice about FID is out of date. FID only looked at the delay before the first input; INP covers whole interactions during the whole visit.

Step 2: measure users, then reproduce in the lab

Field data tells you what is slow, and for whom. Lab data tells you why. You need both, in that order.

import { onCLS, onINP, onLCP } from "web-vitals/attribution";

function report({ name, value, rating, attribution }) {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ name, value, rating, attribution, page: location.pathname });
  navigator.sendBeacon("/vitals", body);
}

onLCP(report);
onINP(report);
onCLS(report);
vitals.js

The web-vitals attribution build tells you which element or interaction was responsible. If you have enough traffic, the Chrome UX Report has field data without any code.

In the lab, repeat every measurement. Eight Lighthouse runs of this site's homepage gave between 280 and 700 ms of blocking time. If you run it once before and once after a change, you're comparing noise.

Step 3: break the metric into parts

LCP has four parts

View this part on the site

  • Time to first byte. Server, redirects, distance.
  • Load delay. Time before the browser even starts fetching the main resource. Usually the largest part, and the most ignored.
  • Load time. The download. This is the only part image compression improves.
  • Render delay. Everything is here, and something stops it being painted: CSS, fonts, or JavaScript.

If the main image is found late, tell the browser early, and never lazy-load it:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high" />
<img src="/hero.avif" fetchpriority="high" width="480" height="480" alt="…" />
html

If the largest element is text, as on this site, images don't matter at all. Here the cause was render delay: text started at opacity: 0 and waited for a script to animate it in. Making content visible by default, as part of a wider rebuild, moved LCP from 4.2 s to around 2 s. No image was the cause.

INP has three parts

Input delay, processing and presentation, each with a different fix. I cover them in Taming INP, with a demo you can feel.

CLS is a list of culprits

Each shift has a source. The usual ones:

  • Images and embeds without width and height.
  • Content inserted above what the user is reading: banners, late ads.
  • Web fonts that swap in with different metrics.

The last is the hardest to see, because it depends on the fonts installed on the visitor's device. My own machine showed a CLS of zero, while a CI runner measured 0.14 for the same build. The full story is worth a read before you trust a local number.

Step 4: fix the largest part, and re-measure

One change at a time, or you won't know which one worked. Write the expected effect down first:

Inlining the critical CSS should cut render delay by about 300 ms on mobile.

If the result disagrees with the prediction, your model of the page is wrong. That is worth more than the 300 ms.

Some things that often turn out to be the largest part:

Symptom Likely cause Fix
High render delay Content hidden until hydration Render visible, animate on top
High load delay Resource found late Preload, or move it into the HTML
Long first task A very long page Shorten it, or use content-visibility
Long handler Synchronous work on click Yield, defer, or move to a worker
Layout shift on load Font swap Preload, or font-display: optional

Step 5: put a budget on it

A fix without a check lasts until the next feature. Budgets belong in CI, where they fail a build instead of a user:

{
  "ci": {
    "assert": {
      "assertions": {
        "categories:accessibility": ["error", { "minScore": 1 }],
        "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 0.1 }],
        "total-blocking-time": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 200 }]
      }
    }
  }
}
lighthouserc.json

Make stable numbers errors and noisy numbers warnings. Bytes are the most stable of all, so this site also fails a build when a page ships more than 170 KB of JavaScript.

Conclusion

Measure real users. Choose one metric. Split it into parts. Fix the largest. Guard it. Then start again, because the largest part is now a different one.

item.title: React Architecture: Where State Lives and Where Boundaries Go
item.description: Most React codebases don't suffer from the wrong folder names. They suffer from state in the wrong place and modules without edges. A practical guide to both.
item.content:encoded:
What architecture is for

A good structure makes one thing cheap: changing your mind. When a requirement moves, how many files move with it? Two questions decide that more than any folder layout. Where does each piece of state live? And what may import what?

Part one: state

Start by not having any

The best state is none. If a value can be calculated from what you already have, calculate it:

// ❌ Two sources of truth that will disagree one day
const [visible, setVisible] = useState(rows);
useEffect(() => setVisible(rows.filter((r) => r.name.includes(query))), [rows, query]);

// ✅ One source, always right
const visible = rows.filter((r) => r.name.includes(query));
tsx

The effect version renders once with stale data before correcting itself. React's own guide, You might not need an effect, is mostly about this pattern.

Then climb one step at a time

View this part on the site

  • Local state for what only one component cares about: an open menu, an input's draft.
  • Lifted state when siblings need it. Move it to the nearest common parent, no higher.
  • The URL for anything a user would want to share or keep after a reload: filters, tabs, the selected row.
  • A server cache, such as TanStack Query, for data that belongs to the server. Copying it into your own store makes you responsible for its freshness.
  • A global store for what is truly global and truly yours: the session, the theme, an unsaved draft across pages.

The URL is the most underused step. Filters in the URL bring back, forward, bookmarks and shared links for free.

Make impossible states impossible

Four booleans describe sixteen combinations, most of them nonsense. A union describes only the real ones:

type Upload =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "uploading"; progress: number }
  | { status: "failed"; reason: string; retry: () => void }
  | { status: "done"; url: string };
ts

You can't read progress from a failed upload, and the compiler lists every place to update when you add "paused". The contact form on this site is a small real example.

Part two: boundaries

Organize by feature

Folders named after kinds of files spread each feature over the whole tree. Deleting one means a treasure hunt.

src/
  features/
    catalog/
      api.ts          requests and response validation
      catalog.ts      domain types and pure logic
      SearchPanel.tsx
      index.ts        the public surface
    glossary/
  shared/             no knowledge of any feature
    ui/
    lib/
text

Two rules hold this up. Features don't import each other's internals, only their index.ts. And shared never imports a feature. Let a linter enforce both, because a rule that lives in a wiki lasts about a month:

"no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
  patterns: [{
    group: ["@/features/*/*"],
    message: "Import from the feature's index instead.",
  }],
}],
eslint.config.mjs

Keep logic out of components

A component is a hard place to test and an easy one to grow. Put decisions into plain functions:

export function canEdit(entity: Entity, user: User): boolean {
  return user.isAdmin || entity.owners.some((o) => o.id === user.id);
}
features/catalog/catalog.ts

Now the rule has a name, a test without rendering, and one home. When permissions become data rather than code, only this function changes.

Validate where data enters

Types describe what you hope the server sends. Check it once, in api.ts, and the rest of the feature can rely on it. Never trust JSON.parse in a render shows what happens otherwise.

Prefer composition to configuration

A component that grows a prop for each new case ends up with thirty. Let callers assemble the parts:

// ❌ Every variation is another prop
<DataTable showSearch searchPlaceholder="…" showExport exportFormats={["csv"]} footerText="…" />

// ✅ The caller decides what's inside
<DataTable rows={rows}>
  <DataTable.Toolbar>
    <Search />
    <ExportButton formats={["csv"]} />
  </DataTable.Toolbar>
  <DataTable.Body />
</DataTable>
tsx

With server components, composition matters even more: passing children through a client component is how server-rendered content stays on the server. See the mental model.

Container and presentational components?

Older guides, including an earlier version of this one, recommended splitting every component into a "container" and a "presentational" half. Hooks made that ceremony unnecessary: a custom hook separates the logic without a wrapper component. Its author says the same. Keep the idea, separate deciding from drawing, and drop the pairs of files.

What to test

Layer Tool Why
Pure logic Unit tests Fast, many cases
A feature Testing Library What the user sees and does
Critical paths Playwright The real browser, the real build

If logic is in plain functions, the first layer covers most of the risk at the lowest price.

Conclusion

Put state as low as possible and lift it only when something breaks. Give every feature an edge, and let a tool guard it. The folder names can be whatever you like.
